[The Bark Blog](https://www.bark.us/blog/)

![Teen slang illustrated with bright words and emojis](https://d12jofbmgge65s.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Teen_Text_Speak_Codes_Blog_Header-1024x536.jpg)[Parent Tech Tips](https://www.bark.us/blog/category/parent-tech-tips/)

# 2026 Teen Slang & Text Codes Every Parent Must Know

The Bark Team  \|

March 01, 2021

- [Facebook](https://www.bark.us/blog/teen-text-speak-codes-every-parent-should-know/#)
- [Twitter](https://www.bark.us/blog/teen-text-speak-codes-every-parent-should-know/#)
- [Email](https://www.bark.us/blog/teen-text-speak-codes-every-parent-should-know/#)

![Teen slang illustrated with bright words and emojis](https://d12jofbmgge65s.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Teen_Text_Speak_Codes_Blog_Header-1024x536.jpg)

_\*\*This blog post was updated on July 20, 2026.\*\*_

## **What is teen text speak and why do kids use it?**

Teen text speak is a mix of abbreviations, acronyms, slang, and coded phrases kids use to communicate digitally, often in ways that fly under a parent's radar. Some of it is casual shorthand like "bet" (I agree) or "no cap" (I'm serious). But some codes, like KMS (kill myself), KYS (kill yourself), or DTF, can signal bullying, sexual activity, depression, or drug use.

The tricky part is that the same phrase can mean something harmless in one conversation and something serious in another. Context matters, and that is exactly what makes this hard to keep up with as a parent.

This guide was built using real-world data from Bark parental controls, which monitors millions of messages across texts, emails, and 30+ social media apps every month. It is updated regularly as new slang surfaces.

**If you found a word or phrase on your child's phone and are not sure what it means, you are in the right place.**

[![](https://d12jofbmgge65s.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/BRK26JAN-Phone-CanIHaveAPhone-mobile-900x368.webp)](https://www.bark.us/app/order/bark-phone#clicked-phone-button?s=wp_wp_textslang "Get the Bark Phone")

Nowadays, it seems like teen slang evolves way more quickly than when we were growing up. New words, phrases, and even emojis with hidden meanings pop up all over the place! And just as quickly as it becomes popular, it becomes out of date just as fast.

At Bark, we know it’s a big task to keep up with [teen slang](https://youtube.com/shorts/4Hlx5S0nhnk?si=0i8eEmdb2P9eQb0j). That's why our [monitoring tool](https://www.bark.us/monitor-content/) uses machine learning algorithms to detect the _context_ of conversations, as opposed to just simple keyword analysis. So when a child texts something like _"bih"_ or _"DTF"_, Bark can pick up from the context that this might be cyberbullying or sexual content, even if on the surface it doesn't seem like anything at all.

In this blog post, we’ve gathered today’s [most popular](https://www.instagram.com/p/CnfMZFvBOS2/) slang terms. Some of this slang you’ll be familiar with, but much of it may surprise you. And we’re always updating this post when new slang surfaces on the web, so save this as a resource to come back to whenever you need it, and be sure to check out our [parenting podcast](https://youtu.be/mJDvbR9dplA?feature=shared) for more insight as you navigate this digital world.

Popular slang terms often are attributed to Gen Z, TikTok, or other parts of popular culture, but it’s important to remember that many of these words and phrases stem from the roots of African American Vernacular English (AAVE).

## **Text Slang Decoded**

- **_21_**— 9+10=21 is an incorrect answer to a math problem, which was first spoken online in a Vine video.

  - _Example:_ “What’s 9+10?” “21.”
- • **6 7** — This refers to a lyric in a song that's used in a video edit of American basketball player LaMelo Ball, who is 6'7".
-  ◦ _Example:_ “He’s like 6 7 in that edit.”
- • **AF** — As f\*\*k
-  ◦ _Example:_ “I’m tired AF.”
- **_A mood_**— A relatable feeling or situation (often shortened to the single word, “mood”)

  - _Example:_ "Skipping plans to stay in bed? A mood."
- **_And that’s on \[something\]_** — Used to indicate that you’ve just shared a truth that needs no further discussion

  - _Example:_ “I’m passing this class, and that’s on everything.”
- **_ASL_** — Age/sex/location

  - _Example:_ "What's your ASL?"
- **_Ate that_**— Means you successfully did something; you pulled it off.

  - _Example:_ “ _I saw your prom pics on Insta, you totally ate that look._”
- **_Aura_** **_points_**— A term used to determine how cool, or not, you are

  - _Example:_ “He lost aura points for tripping like that.”
- **_Aura farming_**—Doing activities to cultivate your aura

  - _Example:_ “Posting gym pics daily is just aura farming.”
- **_Bae_** — Significant other or crush

  - _Example:_ “Going out with bae tonight.”
- **_Basic_** — Someone who is viewed as boring or a conforming person

  - _Example:_ “Pumpkin spice latte again? That’s basic.”
- **_[Beige flag](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/beige-flag-meaning/)_**— A quality or characteristic of a significant other that is weird or off-putting, but not enough to reject them

  - _Example:_ “He claps when the plane lands… kinda a beige flag.”
- _**Bet**_ — A response indicating agreement.

  - _Example: “Wanna go to the store?” “Bet.”_
- **_Beta_**— Someone who is weak or soft, the opposite of an "alpha" or "sigma" type

  - _Example:_ “Stop acting beta, stand up for yourself.”
- **_Bestie_**— “Best friend"; can also be used as a kind of formal address to a stranger

  - _Example:_ “Bestie, you won’t believe this.”
- **Big back**— A body-shaming slang term used to mock a person's physical size or appetite. Though seen in self-deprecating memes, it is frequently used for bullying and harassment.

  - _Example:_ “Stop calling people big back just because they’re eating a second slice of pizza.”
- **_Bih_** — Short form of b\*tch

  - _Example:_ “Move, bih!”
- **_[Body count](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/body-count-meaning/)_** — The number of people someone has slept with

  - _Example:_ “Their body count must be so high."
- **_[Brain rot](https://www.bark.us/blog/what-is-brainrot/)_**— Describes the negative mental effects of consuming too much junk online content. Often used by Gen Z in a self-aware, humorous way.

  - _Example:_ “Scrolling TikTok all day gave me brain rot.”
- **_Brat summer_**— Term based on singer Charli XCX's 2024 album "Brat" released in the summer of 2024. "Brat" in this instance refers to an aesthetic trend defined by heavy partying, cool-girl style, and lime green design

  - _Example:_ “We’re going full brat summer this year.”
- **_Bruh_**— “Bro”; can be used to address anybody

  - _Example:_ “Bruh, what was that for?”
- **BSFR**— Stands for "Be So For Real". Means "Are you serious?" Similar to “don’t lie”, used to express disbelief

  - _Example:_ “Did you just eat my snack? BSFR."
- _**BTS**_ — A Korean boy band especially popular with tweens and teens

  - _Example:_ “She loves BTS, it's her favorite artist.”
- **_Buns_**— Describes something that is of poor quality; similar to calling something "a\*\*"

  - _Example:_ “That movie was buns.”
- **_[Bussin](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/bussin-meaning/)’_** — Awesome

  - _Example:_ “This food is bussin’.”
- _**Cake** —_ Used to describe a large bottom

  - _Example:_ “They got cake.”
- **_[Canon event](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/canon-event-meaning/)_**— A moment in development that will help shape your life or personality

  - _Example:_ “Failing that test was a canon event.”
- _**Cappin’** —_ Lying

  - _Example:_ “You’re cappin’, that didn’t happen.”
- **_Cheeks_**— Describes something that is of poor quality; similar to calling something "a\*\*"

  - _Example:_ “That video game is cheeks.”
- **_[CEO of \[something\]](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/ceo-of-meaning/)_** — To be a representative of some activity or thing.

  - _Example:_ “Taylor is the CEO of sleeping in late.”
- **_[Cheugy](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/cheugy-meaning/)_**— Used to describe someone or something that is basic, out of date, or trying too hard

  - _Example:_ “Skinny jeans? Kinda cheugy now.”
- **_Chopped_**— Ugly or unattractive

  - _Example:_ “That haircut is chopped.”
- **_Choppleganger_**— Someone that looks like you, but more unattractive

  - _Example:_ “That’s your choppleganger."
- **_Chungus_**— Used to jokingly describe something big, silly, or over-the-top

  - _Example:_ “That’s a big chungus cat.”
- **_Chuzz_**— Originating from the slang word "huzz" which refers to hoes, chuzz means "chopped hoes," which is used to describe someone as ugly or unattractive

  - _Example:_ "They're my chuzz."
- **Clock it / clocked**— Used when someone gets called out, signifying agreement.

  - _Example:_ "Why are you always being so rude? "Right, clock it."
- **Cooked**— Refers to being completely doomed, defeated, or stuck in a situation where recovery seems impossible. It can be used as a serious admission of being overwhelmed or in a more playful, exaggerated manner.

  - _Example:_ “I didn’t study for this final at all. I’m cooked.”
- _**Cursed**_ — Used to describe something (usually an online image) that is unsettling or creepy

  - _Example:_ “That image is cursed.”
- **_Crash out_**— Describes an overreaction or tantrum because of something small

  - _Example:_ “He crashed out over nothing.”
- _**Cringe**_ — Causing feelings of embarrassment or awkwardness

  - _Example:_ “That was so cringe.”
- **_D1 crash out_**— Describes a more intense, certifiable crash out

  - _Example:_ “That was a D1 crash out moment.”
- **_Daddy_ —** An attractive man, usually older, who conveys a sense of power and dominance

  - _Example:_ "Wait why is he kind of daddy?"
- _**[Ded](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/what-does-ded-mean/)**_ — Used when something is really funny or embarrassing

  - _Example:_ “That joke got me ded.”
- **_Delulu_**— Short for "delusional" and used when someone has unrealistic ideas about something

  - _Example:_ “You think they like you? That’s delulu.”
- **_Demure_**— While the word itself means modest or shy, the internet has turned it into a trendy aesthetic or lifestyle.

  - _Example:_ "Your outfit is very demure today."
- **Dl trade**— Meaning downlow trade, it’s a phrase used to refer to a person who is “on the downlow” gay/queer, with “trade” signifying that they are generally not considered/easily perceived as a part of the LGBTQIA+ community.

  - _Example:_ "Wait why are they [low-key](https://www.bark.us/learn/low-key-meaning/) giving dl trade?"
- _**Do it for the plot**_— Said to encourage oneself to take a chance on something.

  - _Example:_ I'm going to try out for the basketball team. Even if I don't make it, I'll do it for the plot."
- **Doommaxxing**— Leaning into pessimism or hopelessness as an identity.

  - _Example:_ "Ugh I hate everything right now." "Wow you're really doommaxxing."
- _**Dope**_ — A way to describe something as cool or awesome

  - _Example:_ "That t-shirt is dope!"
- _**Drip**—_ Style, great fashion sense, flashy accessories

  - _Example:_ “He has drip.”
- _**[DTF](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/dtf-meaning/)**_ — Down to f\*ck

  - _Example:_ “They are just looking for someone DTF.”
- **_Egirl / Eboy_ / Eperson**— A young person with emo-inspired, punk-rock style

  - _Example:_ “She’s got that egirl style.”
- **Face card**— A term for the aesthetic appeal of someone's face. If their "face card never declines," it means they are consistently and flawlessly attractive regardless of the setting.

  - _Example:_ “She just woke up and still looks like a model. That face card never declines.”
- **_Facts_**— An emphatic way to acknowledge the truth of someone’s statement

  - _Example:_ "She's so cool." "Yeah, facts."
- _**Fam**_ — Friends

  - _Example:_ “What’s up, fam?”
- **_FBOI_** — F\*\*k boy; a guy just looking for sex

  - _Example:_ “He’s such an fboi.”
- **_Fine shyte_**— Started as "fine as sh\*t," used to describe someone attractive

  - _Example:_ “She’s fine shyte fr.”
- **_FINSTA_** — Fake Instagram account

  - _Example:_ “I posted that on my finsta.”
- **_Fire_**— Amazing

  - _Example:_ “That song is fire.”
- **_FOMO_** — Fear of missing out

  - _Example:_ "I got FOMO missing that party.”
- **_Friggin' packet_**— Originates from an old internet video where a student calls out their teacher for just "handing them a friggin' packet yo" instead of actually teaching them

  - _Example:_ “We just got a friggin’ packet again.”
- **_FWB_** — Friends with benefits

  - _Example:_ “They’re just FWB.”
- _**[Gas](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/gas-meaning/)**_— Can refer to marijuana, be used to describe something that’s cool, or be used as a verb to mean “hype someone up”

  - _Examples:_ “That song is gas.” / “Gas me up!”
- _**Ghosted**_ — Ending a relationship by completely disappearing with no further communication

  - _Example:_ “They ghosted me. I haven't heard from them in days.”
- **_Glaze_**— To hype someone up, often to an insincere, biased, or cringeworthy degree

  - _Example:_ “Stop glazing him.”
- **_Goals_**— Something you want or aspire to

  - _Example:_ “That relationship is goals.”
- **_GOAT_** — Greatest of all time

  - _Example:_ “Michael Jordan is the GOAT.”
- **_Gruzz_**— Originating from the slang word "huzz" which means hoes; gruzz refers to old people

  - _Example:_ "I'm going to meet my gruzz right now, they go to bed early."
- **_GTG_** — Got to go

  - _Example:_ “GTG, talk later.”
- **_[Gucci](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/gucci-meaning/)_** — Something good or cool

  - _Example:_ “We’re Gucci. No issues here.”
- _**GYAT**_— Shortened term for "godd\*\*n" used to express approval or excitement, particularly when one notices a large bottom

  - _Example:_ "That's a GYAT."
- _**Hentai —**_ Graphic anime pornography
- **_High key_** — 1\. Very interested in 2. Actively spreading information

  - _Example:_ “I high key want pizza.”
- **_Hits different_** — When something is better than it normally is because of different circumstances.

  - _Example:_ “A cold soda just hits different when it’s super hot outside.”
- **_Huzz_**— A variation of the word "hoes."

  - _Example:_ “He’s always talking about huzz.”
- **_Hyperpigmentation_** — This term originated from an internet video where a little girl drew a picture of her mom with a black dot on her face. In the video, her mom said, "Is that hyperpigmentation?" and this turned into a meme.
- **_[Ick or Ick Factor](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/ick-meaning/)_**— The feeling you get when your attraction to someone is suddenly flipped to a feeling of disgust

  - _Example:_ "Him riding that scooter gave me the ick."
- **_ISO_** — In search of

  - _Example:_ "ISO of concert tickets."
- **_IYKYK_** — “If you know you know”; meant to imply that there’s an inside joke

  - _Example:_ "That restaurant is really good. IYKYK."
- **_Juul_** — Type of e-cigarette that is small and discreet; ‘pods’ are used for smoking

  - _Example:_ “He’s hitting a Juul.”
- **_Karen_** — Used to refer to an entitled mom

  - _Example:_ “She went full Karen.”
- **_KMS_** — Kill myself

  - _Example:_ "I failed my test, I'm going to KMS."
- **_KYS_** — Kill yourself

  - _Example:_ "You're such a jerk. KYS."
- **_Left no crumbs_**— A phrase that means you did something perfectly

  - _Example:_ "You ate that outfit and left no crumbs."
- **_Let's get sendy_**— Means to "full send" something or go 100%; modern version of "YOLO"

  - _Example:_ "Let's get sendy for the party tonight!"
- **_Lit/Turnt/Turnt Up_** — Something that’s active or popular, can also refer to being stoned or drunk

  - _Example:_ "That party was so lit."
- **_LMP —_** 1 _._ A term that means “like my pic” or 2. Sometimes stands for “lick my p\*\*\*y”
- **_Lock in_**— To be focused and determined to achieve a goal

  - _Example:_ "I need to lock in studying so I pass that test."
- **Lore**— Refers to a person's complex backstory or personal history. Revealing a piece of private info is a "lore drop," while a "lore dump" involves sharing many details at once.

  - _Example:_ “I didn’t know you lived in Japan for three years! That’s such a major lore drop.”
- **_Low key_** — 1\. Somewhat interested in 2. Keeping information secret

  - _Examples:_ “I low key like that.” / "Keep this low key, but I saw them kissing."
- **_Meal_** — Someone who looks good enough to eat. _See also: “Snack” or “snacc”_
  - _Example:_ “He’s a whole meal.”
- **_Mewing_**— The act of making your jawline more defined by putting your tongue to the roof of your mouth.

  - _Example:_ "I'm actually mewing right now."
- **_Mid_**— Insult meaning "low quality" or "average"

  - _Example:_ “That movie was mid.”
- **Mogging**— The act of being significantly more attractive or socially impressive than someone else in a shared space. It can lead to toxic body comparisons despite its frequent use in jokes.

  - _Example:_ “I can’t post this photo because you’re totally mogging me in the background.”
- **Neoboomer** — A younger person who shares ideas and beliefs similar to those commonly associated with boomers.
- **_[No cap](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/no-cap-meaning/)_**— Used to indicate that someone is not lying

  - _Example:_ "I just got $100, no cap."
- **_OFC_** — Short for “of course”

  - _Example:_ "OFC I'm coming."
- **_Ohio_**— Used to describe someone or something that’s weird, bad, or cringe.You’ll also see it alongside “skibidi” and “rizz”.

  - _Example:_ "They're definitely from Ohio."
- **_OK, Boomer_**— Calling out an idea that is outdated or resistant to change
- **_Opp_**— Short for "opponent"; a term for one's enemies

  - _Example:_ "She's my opp."
- **_Peak_**— Describes when something is at its most extreme point, often with a positive connotation.

  - _Example:_ "2018 was peak for Fortnite."
- **Period / on period**— Used to lift someone up, emphasizing that what was said is the final say.

  - _Example:_ "I just got asked to prom." "Period!"
- _**Plug**_ — Term used to refer to someone who can “connect” you with drugs; a drug dealer

  - _Example:_ "My plug can get you marijuana."
- **PMO**— An acronym with two primary meanings depending on the situation: "put me on," which is a request for a recommendation, or "pisses me off," expressing irritation.

  - _Example:_ “Can you PMO to some good new music?” or “John really PMO lately.”
- **_Pookie_**— A term of endearment or nickname that you call your best friend or significant other

  - _Example:_ “Good morning, pookie.”
- **_Preppy_**— Used to refer to a particular aesthetic that involves girly, bright-colored clothes and popular name brands, such as Lululemon and Stanley. It's very similar to the definition of preppy we grew up with, but slightly more refined and "basic".

  - _Example:_ "She dresses preppy."
- **_[Rizz](https://www.bark.us/slang-word/rizz-meaning/)_**— Derived from “charisma." Someone who has “game” when it comes to romantic pursuits.

  - _Example:_ "Taylor has that rizz, they're so charming."
- **_ROTFLMAO_** — Rolling on the floor laughing my ass off

  - _Example: “That meme had me ROTFLMAO.”_
- **_Salty_** — To be bitter or cranky about something

  - _Example:_ "I'm salty she's dating them."
- **_Same_** — “I can relate”

  - _Example:_ "I feel so tired." "Same."
- **_Shading_** — Where teens gossip about another party without naming them; also “throw shade” means to talk about someone

  - _Example:_ “She was shading him online.”
- **_Ship_** — Short for “relationship”; also used as a verb to indicate a desire to see two people together.

  - _Example:_ "I ship Taylor and Jamie."
- _**Sigma**_— Someone who is a lone-wolf type, independent but still strong. As opposed to the more dominant "Alpha" male type.

  - _Example:_ "He's so sigma!"
- **_Simp_**— Somebody who tries very hard and does a lot for their crush.

  - _Example:_ "You got Sarah 3 dozen roses? Stop being such a simp."
- _**Sis —**_ Short for “sister” but can be used to address anybody; usually used to express that drama has occurred

  - _Example:_ "Sis I need to tell you something."
- **Situationship _**—**_** a romantic or sexual relationship that doesn’t have a clear definition or commitment.

  - _Example:_ "They have a weird situationship thing going on right now."
- _**Skeet** —_ To ejaculate
- **_Skibidi_** _—_An adjective that can have multiple meanings such as “cool,” “dumb,” or “bad." It comes from meme culture and originates from “Skibidi Toilet,” a popular YouTube video. It's not unlike the nonsense video from the early '00s "Peanut Butter Jelly Time."

  - _Example:_ "That's so skibidi."
- **_Skibidi toilet_**—A surreal animated video featuring a singing toilet. It's not supposed to make sense or any sense, it's just a funny video popular with Gen Alpha.

  - _Example:_ "You're so skibidi toilet."
- **_Slaps_**— Used to express that something is awesome.

  - _Example:_ "This burrito slaps."
- **_Slay_**— Used to describe something as good or awesome.

  - _Example:_ "That dress is so slay."
- **_Smash_** — Means to have casual sex

  - _Example:_ "I would smash him."
- **_SMDH_** — Shaking my damn head

  - _Example:_ "Did you actually say that to him? [SMDH](https://www.bark.us/learn/what-does-smdh-mean-text/)."
- **_SMH_** — “Shaking my head,” meaning “I don’t believe it” or “that’s so dumb”

  - _Example:_ "Don't be rude SMH."
- **_Snack_** — Describes an attractive person

  - _Example:_ "Oh wow, they're a snack."
- **_Snatched_** — On point, very good, or well styled. Can also refer to someone's waist size.

  - _Examples:_ “That outfit is snatched.” / "Your waist is snatched girl!"
- **Soft-Blocking IRL**— Avoiding someone in real life (IRL) without direct confrontation.

  - _Example:_ "I'm soft-blocking him IRL. It's just so awkward now."
- **Spiral Posting**— Rapid, emotional social media posting during distress.

  - _Example:_ "Did you Sarah was spiral posting yesterday? I was worried about her."
- **_Squad_**— Close friend group

  - _Example:_ "I'll pull up with the squad."
- _**Stan —**_ A teen slang term meaning an overzealous or obsessive fan of a particular celebrity

  - _Example:_ "Is that Charli XCX? OMG I'm her stan!!"
- **_STFU_** — Short for “shut the f\*\*k up,” can be used as an expression of disbelief or to cyberbully

  - _Examples:_ "I saw her at the party last night." "STFU." / "STFU, you're so annoying!"
- _**Sus**_— Short for "suspicious." Popularized by the Among Us game.

  - _Example:_ "Why is he acting so sus?"
- **_Swoop_** — To be picked up in an automobile

  - _Example:_ "I'll swoop you."
- **_SYBAU_**— Stands for "shut your b\*tch @ss up"

  - _Example:_ "SYBAU no you didn't."
- **_TBH_** — To be honest

  - _Example:_ "TBH, I don't really want to go out today."
- _**Tea**_ — Gossip or interesting news shared between friends

  - _Example:_ "I have tea about Taylor and her new situationship."
- **_Thicc_** — Having an attractive, curvy body

  - _Example:_ "Wow she's so thicc."
- **_TF_** — The f\*\*k

  - _Example:_ “Who TF you think are?”
- **_Thirsty_** — Desperate for attention, usually sexual attention

  - _Example:_ “He’s acting thirsty. He won't stop asking to hang out.”
- **_Thot_** — Stands for “that ho over there” and is often used instead of “slut”

  - _Example:_ “He called her a thot.”
- **Touch grass** — A phrase used to tell someone they need to log off and reconnect with reality. It’s often used as an insult or a teasing reminder for those too deep in digital drama.

  - _Example:_ “You’ve been arguing about a TikTok for three hours. Please go touch grass.”
- **_Trap phone_**— Also called a burner phone, this is an older, hand-me-down smartphone that kids trade or sell with each other. Kids who get their phones taken away by their parents may seek out a trap phone to have easy internet access (provided they can connect it to Wi-Fi).

  - _Example:_ "Their parents took away their phone so they got a trap phone."
- **_Trash_**— Terrible or unacceptable

  - _Example:_ "That basketball game was trash. My team lost so badly."
- **_Unc_**— A term that refers to an older, typically male, figure. It can also refer more generally to any older person or someone who is out of touch with current trends.

  - _Example:_ “Unc don’t know trends.”
- **_V_**— “Very”

  - Example: “That’s v cool.”
- **_Vibing_** — Chilling out, having a good time, or identifying with a certain kind of energy

  - _Example:_ "We were just vibing last night."
- **_WAP_** — Wet @ss p\*ssy, also a popular song by Cardi B and Megan Thee Stallion
- **Winter arc** _—_A period of intense discipline and self-improvement during the last few months of the year, focusing on goals like fitness or academics before the new year.

  - _Example:_ “I’m starting my winter arc early so I can hit my gym goals by January.”
- _**Woke**_ — Socially or politically conscious

  - _Example:_ "You're so woke."
- **WYLL**— Stands for "what you look like." Often used by strangers online to ask for photos, so teens are encouraged to be careful when they see this acronym.

  - _Example:_“I matched with someone on Snap and the first thing they sent was ‘WYLL?’”
- **_YAAS_**— A very emphatic yes

  - _Example:_ "My last paycheck was so big!" "YAAS!!"
- **Yapping** — Talking for a long time, usually about topics that others find trivial. While it can be dismissive, teens also use it to lightheartedly describe their own talkative nature.

  - _Example:_ “I know I’m yapping, but let me finish telling you what happened at the mall.”
- **_YEET_** — 1\. A very strong word for yes 2. To throw something

  - _Example:_ "I just yeeted my shoes across the room."
- **_Zaddy_** — A well-dressed, attractive man of any age

  - _Example:_ "He's kind of a zaddy."

## **Older Teen Slang Terms**

- **_420_** — Marijuana reference

  - _Example:_ “It’s 420, you know what time it is.”
- **_11:11_** _— P_ opular time to make a wish

  - _Example:_ "11:11, make a wish!"
- **_ASB_ —** As balls.

  - _Example:_ "I’m high asb."
- **_Chad_**— A hyper-sexual young man

  - _Example:_ “He acts like such a Chad.”
- **_Chill_**— Relaxed or laid back

  - _Example:_ “He’s really chill.”
- _**Coney**_ — Slang for “penis”

  - _Example:_ “They were making jokes about his coney.”
- **_CYA_** — “Cover your ass” or “see ya”

  - _Examples:_ "CYA when he's around, he's scary." / "CYA later!"
- **_Dabbing_** — Refers to concentrated doses of cannabis; also a dance craze

  - _Examples:_ “He was dabbing marijuana at the party.” / "He kept hitting the dab."
- _**Dongle** —_ Slang for “penis”

  - _Example:_ “They kept joking about his dongle.”
- _**HEAF**_ — An acronym for “High Expectations Asian Father”

  - _Example:_ “My dad is such a HEAF about grades.”
- _**Hulk**_ — A 2mg generic benzodiazepine bar, which is green

  - _Example:_ “He said he took a Hulk.”
- **_ILY_** — I love you

  - _Example:_ "ILY so much boo!"
- **_IRL_** — In real life

  - _Example:_ "I'm going to meet up with her for the first time IRL today."
- **_JK_** — Just kidding

  - _Example:_ "I'm JK no worries at all."
- **_Netflix and chill_** — Getting together and hooking up

  - _Example:_ "Do you want to Netflix and chill later?"
- _**OKURRR**_ — Variation of “OKAY” made popular by rapper Cardi B who defines it as something that is said to affirm when someone is being put in their place

  - _Example:_ "You told them! OKURRR."
- _**School Bus**_ — A 2mg Xanax bar, which is yellow

  - _Example:_ He just ate a school bus."
- **_SH_** — Sh\*\* happens

  - _Example:_ "No worries, SH."
- **_Snapstreak_** _—_ Created when friends send snaps every day, creating a streak

  - _Example:_ "We’ve got a 200-day Snapstreak.”
- **_Spam_** — A fake social media account

  - _Example:_ "I have a spam account where I post a bunch."
- _**TDTM**_ — Talk dirty to me

  - _Example:_ "He TDTM last night."
- **_VSCO girl_** — A style characterized by Hydro Flasks, Crocs, and scrunchies

  - _Example:_ “She dresses like a VSCO girl.”
- **_WTF_** — What the f\*\*k?

  - _Example:_ “WTF was that?”
- **_WYA_** — Where you at?

  - _Example:_ "I'm here, WYA?"
- **_WYD_** — What you doing?

  - _Example:_ "WYD tomorrow?"
- **_WUF_** — Where you from?

  - _Example:_ "I'm from Indanapolis, WUF?"

### **Teen Slang Emoji Icons**

Pretty frequently, kids opt for emojis instead of typing out full words, and understanding the meaning behind these teen lingo emojis can help parents stay in the loop. Here’s a helpful list of some of the most popular [teen slang emojis](https://www.bark.us/blog/emoji-slang-guide/) decoded.

Keeping up with internet slang can sometimes feel like learning a whole new language, especially with the rate at which new slang words come and go. In 2025 alone, the Oxford English Dictionary added over 500 words and phrases\[1\], crowning ‘rage bait’ their word of the year\[2\] – much to many people’s surprise.

One minute we’re coming to terms with ‘6-7’ and ‘rage bait’, and the next we’re being told that ‘the saxophones are getting louder’, wondering what it is that’s actually happening.

So, we’ve rounded up some of the most viral words and phrases we’ve heard this year, creating a cheat sheet to 2026 slang, because nobody wants to be ‘cringe’.

## **Preply’s 2026 slang dictionary**

![Preply’s 2026 slang dictionary](https://preply.com/wp-content/uploads/Preplys-2026-slang-dictionary.png)

From TikTok viral ‘boy kibble’ to the World Cup’s ‘Mbappé special’, we analysed the new and quirky slang terms that have somehow made their way into our everyday conversations, as Madeline Enos, language trends expert here at Preply, shares expert insights into the phrases.

![](https://preply.com/wp-content/themes/peply-blog-v4.0/assets/img/del/campaign__Kariamny.png)

## **Emerging slang trends for 2026**

1. **Biggest year-on-year spike:** ‘The saxophones are getting louder’ surged 12,959% in search interest in 2026 – no other slang word or phrase tracked came close.
2. **Highest search volume overall:** ‘LARP’ pulled in 1.1 million worldwide searches in 2026, making it the most-searched slang term on this list by raw volume.

### **January**

#### **1\. Lowkenuinely**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘lowkenuinely’ peaked in January 2026, reaching 22,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Lowkenuinely’ means to tell the truth or share information in a sincere, calm, or laid-back way.

**Where did ‘lowkenuinely’ come from?** _“‘Lowkenuinely’ is a combination of the slang phrase ‘lowkey’, meaning to be quiet or subtle, and ‘genuinely’, meaning sincerely. The phrase originates from TikTok, where Gen Z may say ‘I lowkenuinely love this song’, being a softer alternative to ‘actually’ or ‘seriously’, which are typically used to express a strong opinion.”_

### **February**

#### **2\. Cortisol spike**

**_**_Worldwide searches for ‘cortisol spike’ were up by 161% in three months, hitting 81,000 searches in February 2026._**_**

**Preply’s definition:**‘Cortisol spike’ is a viral internet joke used to describe moments of shock, embarrassment, or awkwardness.

**Where did ‘cortisol spike’ come from?** _“The phrase ‘cortisol spike’ originated as a joke on X in early 2025, used humorously to refer to stressful or embarrassing situations. In early 2026, the phrase became a widespread viral internet expression, often paired with a fake or exaggerated ‘cortisol meter’ meme. Now, the slang phrase has evolved further into two variations: ‘high cortisol’, referring to high anxiety and stress, while ‘low cortisol’ refers to calm or nonchalant behaviour.”_

### **March**

#### **3\. Boy kibble**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘boykibble’ spiked by 123% in March, hitting 29,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Boy kibble’ is a viral social media food featuring simple, high-protein meals, typically including ground meat and white rice.

**Where did ‘boy kibble’ come from?** _“Boy kibble is a new playful take on ‘girl dinner’. Where ‘girl dinner’ typically consists of random snacks or bits and pieces from the fridge, ‘boy dinner’ is the opposite, made up of plain, highly-functioning ingredients. The contrast between ‘girl dinner’ and the new ‘boy kibble’ demonstrates Gen Z’s natural embrace of protein, in a tongue-in-cheek, humorous way by comparing ground beef and white rice to dog food.”_

#### **4\. Future Faking**

**_UK searches for ‘future faking’ up by 94% on the previous year in March 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Future faking’ refers to a behaviour where someone provides empty promises for the future to get something they presently want.

**Where did ‘future faking’ come from?** _“‘Future faking’ is a modern term which acts to summarise a large set of behaviours displayed early in a relationship. This may reflect a broader cultural shift within modern dating towards passive, non-committal language.”_

#### **5\. The saxophones are getting louder**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘the saxophones are getting louder’ were up by 12,959% over the previous year in 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘The saxophones are getting louder’ means that something bad, negative, or inevitable is getting closer.

**Where did ‘the saxophones are getting louder’ come from?** _“The ‘saxophones getting louder’ grew from the famous 1991 film, Boyz n the Hood, where swelling saxophones foreshadow a dramatic shooting. Now, with TikTok users making videos to the sound, it’s become a viral meme used to signal impending doom, from falling down the stairs to accidentally spending too much money in a restaurant.”_

### **April**

#### **6\. Looksmaxxing**

**_**_Worldwide searches for ‘looksmaxxing’ were up by 149% since January 2026, hitting 399,000 searches in April 2026._**_**

**Preply’s definition:**‘Looksmaxxing’ refers to trying to improve someone’s physical appearance or attractiveness as much as possible.

**Where did  ‘looksmaxxing’  come from?** _“‘Looksmaxxing’ emerged from TikTok and social media online subcultures focused on maximising physical appearance through facial features, height, jawlines, and skin. This slang suffix (often used as -maxxing) has rapidly evolved into a much wider cultural phenomenon, driven by social media algorithms and digital-first communication.”_

#### **7\. 7×7=49**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘7×7 49’ were up by 565% on the previous year, hitting 21,000 searches in April 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘7x’7=49’ is a viral TikTok meme and shorthand slang used to describe something or someone that is extremely attractive.

**Where did ‘7×7=49’ come from?** _“The equation ‘7×7=49’ became TikTok viral after users jokingly shared that they found the equation attractive, transforming an ordinary maths equation into a hilarious internet meme. While it may seem absurd, this phrase is Gen Z’s new way of saying ‘hear me out’, giving everyday words, or even numbers, a new meaning through humour and shared understanding.”_

#### **8\. Everything Hallelujah**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘everything hallelujah’ were up by 1,519% on the previous year, hitting 191,000 searches in April 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Everything hallelujah’ is typically used after a short sentence or statement to celebrate everyday micro-wins and express gratitude.

**Where did ‘everything hallelujah’ come from?** _“Following Justin Bieber’s viral Coachella performance of ‘Everything Hallelujah’, fans began using the phrase as a casual suffix, adding ‘hallelujah’ to the end of simple sentences. Even Hailey Bieber jumped in on the trend, posting on TikTok ‘Rhodes eye patches hallelujah’ and ‘sweet treat hallelujah’, as fans embrace the phrase as a simple way to express gratitude.”_

### **May**

#### **9\. Mogging**

**_**_Worldwide searches for ‘mogging’ were up by 203% since January 2026, hitting 566,000 searches in May 2026._**_**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘‘Mogging’ is a viral TikTok phrase meaning to outshine or look significantly better than someone else.

**Where did ‘mogging’ come from?** _“The slang phrase ‘mogging’ has an interesting history, growing from the acronym ‘AMOG’, meaning ‘Alpha Male Of the Group’, which originated from pick-up artist communities and bodybuilding forums. In recent years, the term has spread across social media platforms, particularly TikTok, as Gen Z picked up the slang phrase ‘mogging’ and made it their own. The phrase now refers to outperforming others in physical appearance, often used jokingly online.”_

#### **10\. You the birthday**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘you the birthday’ peaked in May 2026, hitting 910,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘You the birthday’ is a compliment to say that someone is the ‘main character’ or main attention of the room.

**Where did ‘you the birthday’ come from?** _“‘You the birthday’ is a classic example of Gen Z’s vague and quirky communication style. Essentially, it’s another ‘6-7’ case, where the phrase itself is commonly used without real meaning acting as a compliment.”_

### **June**

#### **11\. LARP**

**_Worldwide Google searches for ‘LARP’ were up by 195% over the previous year, hitting 1,100,000 searches in April 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘LARP’ is used as an adjective to describe someone who is perceived to be performative.

**Where did ‘LARP’ come from?** _“The phrase ‘LARP’ is originally derived from the acronym meaning Live Action Role Play, a hobby where individuals dress up and act out fictional scenarios. Now, ‘LARP’ has evolved and become a prominent fixture in internet slang, showing how quickly a niche acronym can enter everyday urban lingo. The transition from an acronym to an adjective clearly demonstrates social media’s significant impact on real-world language trends, where online subcultures drive language change.”_

### **July**

#### **12\. Mbappé special**

**_Worldwide Google searches for ‘Mbappé special’ skyrocketed by 233% in July, reaching 14,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** The ‘Mbappé special’ simply translates to ‘nothing’, used playfully by users on social media when someone or something has quite literally done nothing.

**Where did ‘Mbappé special’ come from?** _“The ‘Mbappé special’ originates from a viral interview with Vanity Fair, where, after revealing he is learning to cook, Kylian Mbappé is asked what the ‘Mbappé special’ is. The football star went viral after responding ‘for example, nothing’, gaining 19.4 million views. This viral meme stretched beyond social media, with football fans using the ‘Mbappé special’ to express disappointment in players’ performances at the World Cup.”_

#### **13\. Quiet on the creek**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘quiet on the creek’ spiked by 8,300% in July 2026, reaching 512,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** The phrase ‘quiet on the creek’ means to be quiet or keep something to yourself.

**Where did ‘quiet on the creek’ come from?** _“The TikTok-born slang originates from a viral video by American rapper Saucy Santana, who on a TikTok live, while eating food, explained ‘I used to go fishing when I was a little girl, you gotta be real quiet on the creek’._

_“The expression directly draws from the idea that if somebody is too loud while fishing, they’ll scare the fish away. As internet slang, users came to interpret the phrase as meaning to keep their plans, achievements, or relationships private, rather than public.”_

### **August**

#### **14\. Polyester**

_**Worldwide searches for ‘polyester slang’ spiked by 141% in a single week in August 2026, up by 1,292% over the previous year.**_

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Polyester’ is used as a critique to call out content that is perceived as low-quality, generic, or inauthentic online.

**Where did ‘polyester’ come from?** _“‘Polyester’ is the internet’s latest slang term, giving a familiar word a new meaning. Traditionally, polyester is a synthetic material commonly used in affordable (and often mass-produced) clothing, but now it’s taking on a whole new meaning. The term has gained traction among Gen Z, calling out polyester lifestyles, videos, and even people, reflecting a wider Gen Z preference for authenticity over polished perfection online.”_

#### **15\. Meat Proxy**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘meat proxy’ were up by 1,847% over the previous year, hitting 14,000 searches in August 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Meat proxy’ refers to someone who forwards or uses AI-generated content without reading, understanding, or editing it.

**Where did ‘meat proxy’ come from?** _“‘Meat proxy’ is a quickly emerging corporate and tech slang phrase for AI users. Widely thought to be coined by developer Niklas Guhn, the phrase reflects a wider attitude towards artificial intelligence in professional environments, where ‘meat proxy’ becomes a way to express frustration with the disappearance of authenticity in light of more AI content.”_

### **September**

#### **16\. That’s so AI**

_**_Worldwide searches for ‘that’s so AI’ were up by 178% over the previous year, hitting 21,000 searches in September 2026._**_

**Preply’s definition:**‘That’s so AI’ is a popular Gen Alpha insult referring to something that is fake or low-quality.

**Where did ‘that’s so AI’ come from?** _“The slang phrase ‘that’s so AI’ grew from Gen Alpha’s perception of artificial intelligence as low-quality and fake-looking. Now, ‘that’s so AI’ doesn’t necessarily mean that something was actually created with AI. More young people are increasingly using the phrase as an insult to call out fake, unbelievable, or phoney behaviour more broadly.”_

## What 2026 slang tells us about language

Slang might come and go, but it shows us something bigger: language never stands still. From TikTok trends to football interviews, the words we use evolve with our culture, communities, and conversations. Keeping up isn’t about knowing every viral phrase. It’s about understanding how people really communicate. And whether you’re learning a new language or simply trying to make sense of your feed, every new expression is another way to connect.

![](https://preply.com/wp-content/themes/peply-blog-v4.0/assets/img/del/frame-levels.png)

# Glossary of 2020s slang

Glossary of 2020s slang

"Glossary of Generation Z slang" and "Glossary of Generation Alpha slang" redirect here. For youth slang in general, see [Youth slang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_slang "Youth slang").

|     |     |
| --- | --- |
| [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Text_document_with_red_question_mark.svg/120px-Text_document_with_red_question_mark.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Text_document_with_red_question_mark.svg) | Some of this article's [listed sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") **may not be [reliable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")**. Please help improve this article by looking for better, more reliable sources. Unreliable citations may be challenged and removed._(February 2026)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ |

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Hilt_Boling_and_Family_Tour_NASA%27s_Kennedy_Space_Center_%28NHQ20260403_admin_0004%29.jpg/500px-Hilt_Boling_and_Family_Tour_NASA%27s_Kennedy_Space_Center_%28NHQ20260403_admin_0004%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilt_Boling_and_Family_Tour_NASA's_Kennedy_Space_Center_(NHQ20260403_admin_0004).jpg)" [6-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6-7_meme "6-7 meme")" became a slang term in March – November 2025.

English-language slang used or popularized in the 2020s, usually by [Generation Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_Z "Generation Z") (Gen Z) or by [Generation Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_Alpha "Generation Alpha") (Gen Alpha), differs from that of earlier generations.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-ft-2) Ease of communication via social media and other internet outlets has facilitated its rapid proliferation, creating "an unprecedented variety of linguistic variation", according to Danielle Abril of _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")_.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-ft-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-CS-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-4) [Self-deprecating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-deprecation "Self-deprecation") irony is often a prevalent factor in its use.

Many Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang terms were not originally coined by their generation but were already in use or simply became more mainstream. Much of what is considered Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang originates from [African-American Vernacular English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_Vernacular_English "African-American Vernacular English"), [Black queer ball culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_culture "Ball culture"), and [incel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incel "Incel") culture.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-ft-2)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-7)

This is a [dynamic list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Lists#Dynamic_lists "Wikipedia:WikiProject Lists") and may never be able to satisfy particular standards for completeness. You can help by [editing the page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Glossary_of_2020s_slang "Special:EditPage/Glossary of 2020s slang") to add missing items, with references to [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources").

## A

| Term | Definition | References |

| acoustic/artistic | [Algospeak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algospeak "Algospeak") forms of the word " [autistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autistic "Autistic")." Used as insults to call someone stupid, in the same manner as " [retarded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retard_(pejorative) "Retard (pejorative)")" has come to be used. | [\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-8) |
| [and I oop](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/and%20I%20oop "wikt:and I oop") | Used to express shock, embarrassment, and/or amusement. Often associated with [VSCO girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VSCO_girl "VSCO girl") alongside ' [sksksk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#S)'. | [\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-independent-10) |
| aura | An individual's current reputation or charisma. Cultivating aura is known as [aura farming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aura_farming "Aura farming"). | [\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-11) |
| ate | To have performed well or extremely good at something. | [\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-12) |

## B

| Term | Definition | References |
| --- | --- | --- |
| baddie | A confident, stylish, and attractive woman or girl. | [\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-13) |
| ball knowledge | niche or uncommon knowledge, usually niche references, often in pop culture. Alternative forms include "elite ball knowledge" or "knowing ball". | [\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-14) |
| based | Originated from rapper [Lil B The BasedGod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_B "Lil B"), who defined it as "...being yourself. Not being scared of what people think about you. Not being afraid to do what you wanna do." More contemporary use has been to express approval of someone or agreeing with another's opinion, similar to the usage of " [W](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#W)". The term is often used by the [alt-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-right "Alt-right"). | [\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-BASED-KQED-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-18) |
| [basic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_(slang) "Basic (slang)") | those who prefer mainstream products, trends, and music. Derived from the term " [basic bitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_bitch "Basic bitch")". | [\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-UK-21) |
| bar(s) | A lyric in a [rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rap "Rap") song that is considered excellent. A talented rapper may be said to "drop bars" or be "spitting bars", sometimes shortened to just "spitting". | [\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-22) |
| BDE | Abbreviation for " [big dick energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_dick_energy "Big dick energy")": confidence and ease. | [\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-23) |
| Bean Soup Theory | A specific phenomenon described as a 'What about me' effect. An individual watches a video that doesn't pertain to them, but finds a way to make it about them anyway. Stems from a 2023 TikTok recipe for bean soup by @vibingranolamom with commenters saying "What if I don't like beans?" | [\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-24) |
| beige flag | A behavior or personality trait that is neither good nor bad. Derived from the relationship terms " [green flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flag "Green flag")" and " [red flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_flag_(idiom) "Red flag (idiom)")". | [\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-RG-25) |
| bet | Agreeing to something; yes; okay; sure. | [\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-26) |
| bffr | Acronym for "be fucking for real". | [\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-27) |
| big back | an overweight and gluttonous person. | [\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-28) |
| big yikes | something embarrassing or cringeworthy, particularly in response to an offensive comment. | [\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-29) |
| big yahu | Nickname for [Israeli Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Prime_Minister "Israeli Prime Minister") [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu"), sometimes used to portray Netanyahu as a spiritual being who assists in minor inconveniences. | [\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-30) |
| bop | (1) A [derogatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pejorative "Pejorative") term, usually for females, suggesting excessive flirtatiousness or promiscuity. (2) An exceptionally good song. (3) An acronym for "baddie on point", meaning someone who uses their appearance to make money. | (1)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-31) (2)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-33) (3)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-34) |
| [brain rot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain_rot "Brain rot") (or brainrot) | The state of being detached from the real world as a result of consuming [hyper-stimulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulation "Stimulation") or [chronically online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronically_online "Chronically online") content, especially when characterized by online buzzwords (e.g., " [skibidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skibidi_Toilet "Skibidi Toilet")", " [fanum tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanum_tax "Fanum tax")", " [rizz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizz "Rizz")", etc). Derived from the idea that one's brain would "rot" from consuming too much stimulating, addictive or degenerate content. | [\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-36)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-37) |

Bruh resurged once more in the late 2010s, entering heavy use in [Gen Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gen_Z "Gen Z") & [Gen Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gen_Alpha "Gen Alpha") slang. | [\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-fm-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-40) |
| buns | Something that is considered bad or low quality. | [\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-41) |
| bussin' | Extremely good, excellent. Originated from African-American vernacular for delicious food. | [\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-42) |
| bussy | Portmanteau of "boy" and "pussy" (slang for the [vagina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vagina "Vagina")). ## C

# Top 25 TikTok Slang Terms in 2025

5 min readJune 17, 2025

You’re scrolling through [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@ohlaschools) and suddenly see phrases like “ _delulu_,” “ _soft life,_” or “ _caught a vibe_.” And you wonder—is this even English? Well, it is! As an **ESL student** in 2025, learning TikTok slang can make English feel more natural, relatable, and fun.

In this blog, you’ll find out what **TikTok slang** really means, explore the top trending terms of 2025, and get tips to use them confidently.

![TikTok Slang in 2025](https://www.ohla.com/blog/wp-content/smush-webp/2025/06/1-2.jpg.webp)

_Whether you’re new to TikTok or just want to sound more like a local, this guide is for you!_

## Why [ESL Students](https://www.ohla.com/) Should Learn TikTok Slang

TikTok is more than just entertainment or online trends—it’s a space where real, everyday English is heard and learned. In particular, [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@ohlaschools) slang reflects how _younger generations_ communicate today, offering international students an authentic glimpse into modern language use.

By understanding these terms, students not only gain confidence to connect with native speakers but also begin to grasp cultural references that go beyond the classroom. More importantly, it keeps English learning fun, engaging, and relevant— **no longer limited to traditional textbooks** or rigid lessons.

Watching just a few videos a day can improve pronunciation, expand vocabulary, and boost listening skills, all in a matter of minutes.

## Top 25 TikTok Slang Terms in 2025

We’ve put together a list of **25 TikTok slang terms** that are relevant and trending this year. These are the words and phrases you’ve likely seen (or will soon see) all over your [For You Page](https://www.tiktok.com/foryou?lang=en).

Whether you’re trying to understand Gen Z, [boost your English](https://www.ohla.com/blog/top-books-every-esl-student-should-read/), or just stay in the loop, this list is for you.

#### 1\. Main Character Energy

**Definition:** Acting like the center of attention; the star of the story.

**Example:** _“After her breakup, she was in her main character era.”_

#### 2\. Delulu

**Definition:** Short for “delusional,” this slang is used when someone believes something unrealistic (usually about love, fame, or success).

**Example:** _“He thinks his celebrity crush will find him one day. He’s totally delulu.”_

#### 3\. It’s Giving \[X\]

**Definition:** Used to describe the overall vibe, look or mood of something.

**Example:** _“They walked into the party wearing all pink—it’s giving Margot Robbie in Barbie.”_

#### 4\. Soft Launch

**Definition:** A subtle or quiet reveal (usually of a relationship or project).

**Example:** _“She posted his shoes in her story—classic soft launch. They’re definitely dating.”_

#### 5\. Core Memory

**Definition:** A moment that’s unforgettable and stays with you.

**Example:** _“That picnic by the lake? Core memory.”_

#### 6\. POV

**Definition:** Short for “Point of View.” On TikTok, it’s used to show a scene from someone’s perspective.

**Example:** _“POV: You’re in Paris for 24 hours.”_

#### 7\. Aesthetic

**Definition:** Used to describe a pleasing, stylish or put together look.

**Example:** _“Her Instagram page is peak aesthetic.”_

#### 8\. Glow Up

**Definition:** A big, noticeable, and positive personal transformation—often in appearance, confidence, or lifestyle.

**Example:** _“We’ve all had a major glow up since high school.”_

#### 9\. Vibe Check

**Definition:** Testing or noticing the mood or energy of a situation or place.

**Example:** _“Vibe check: Checking out the party early before committing to staying.”_

#### 10\. No Thoughts, Just Vibes

**Definition:** Feeling peaceful or relaxed.

**Example:** _“Staring at the ocean this morning—no thoughts, just vibes.”_

#### 11\. Rizz

**Definition:** Short for “charisma”, often used to describe someone’s flirting skills or charm.

**Example:** _“He’s got major rizz—everyone loves him on TikTok.”_

#### 12\. Plot Twist

**Definition:** An unexpected turn of events.

**Example:** _“Plot twist: the quiet one was the best dancer.”_

#### 13\. Normalize

**Definition:** To make something seem normal, accepted, or part of everyday life, even if it wasn’t before.

**Example:** _“Let’s normalize rest without guilt.”_

#### 14\. Big \[X\] Energy

**Definition:** Strong presence of a specific vibe or trait.

**Example:** _“They’re giving big vacation energy.”_

#### 15\. Living Rent-Free

**Definition:** Something or someone that’s constantly on your mind.

**Example:** _“This song is living rent-free in my head.”_

#### 16\. Yeet

**Definition:** To throw something quickly or forcefully, often without much care. It also shows energy or approval in a moment.

**Example:** _“He yeeted it across the room.”_

#### 17\. Situationship

**Definition:** A romantic or flirtatious relationship with no clear labels, commitment, or expectations. It goes beyond a friendship but doesn’t reach the level of a formal relationship.

**Example:** _“We’re not dating… it’s more of a situationship.”_

#### 18\. In My \[X\] Era

**Definition:** A playful way of saying “a new chapter in one’s life.”

**Example:** _“I’m in my wellness era.”_

#### 19\. Caught a Vibe

**Definition:** Felt a good mood or connection.

**Example:** _“We caught a vibe at the beach last night.”_

#### 20\. Soft Girl / Soft Life

**Definition:** Embracing gentle, relaxed living.

**Example:** _“I’m done being a night nurse. I’m ready for my soft life.”_

#### 21\. Out of Pocket

**Definition:** Means someone is acting wild, inappropriate, or out of line

**Example:** _“That joke was so out of pocket.”_

#### 22\. Real Ones Know

**Definition:** Only insiders will understand.

**Example:** _“Real ones know. Who directed Star Wars?”_

#### 23\. Silent Slay

**Definition:** Impressing others quietly or without trying.

**Example:** _“She just walked in and owned the room—silent slay.”_

#### 24\. Cozy Vibes

**Definition:** Warm, relaxing atmosphere.

**Example:** _“Rain, tea, and fuzzy socks—cozy vibes only.”_

#### 25\. I Can’t (Even)

**Definition:** Something is overwhelmingly funny or cute.

**Example:** _“Your puppy? I can’t even 🥺.”_

## Final Thoughts

Slang terms help [international students](https://www.ohla.com/) connect with modern English. As a result, conversations feel more natural and relatable with younger natives.

By learning _popular TikTok expressions_, you not only understand the language but also the culture behind it. So next time you’re scrolling TikTok, listen closely—there’s always something new to learn!

December 12, 2024

# Teens, Social Media and Technology 2024

## YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat remain widely used among U.S. teens; some say they’re on these sites almost constantly

[X](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#)
[Facebook](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#)
[Threads](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#)
[LinkedIn](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#)
[WhatsApp](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#)

- [Mail](https://%25mail%25/)

[Add Us On Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=https://www.pewresearch.org)

By [Michelle Faverio](https://www.pewresearch.org/staff/michelle-faverio/) and [Olivia Sidoti](https://www.pewresearch.org/staff/olivia-sidoti/)

Table of Contents

1. [Teens, Social Media and Technology 2024](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/)   - [How often do teens visit online platforms?](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#how-often-do-teens-visit-online-platforms)
   - [How does the use of online platforms differ across demographic groups?](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#how-does-the-use-of-online-platforms-differ-across-demographic-groups)
   - [How much time are teens spending online?](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#how-much-time-are-teens-spending-online)
   - [What devices do teens have access to at home?](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#what-devices-do-teens-have-access-to-at-home)
2. [Acknowledgments](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-tech-acknowledgments/)
3. [Methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-tech-methodology/)

![An image of two teenage boys use their smartphones in Vail, Colorado. (Robert Alexander/Getty Images)](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_featured.png)Two teenage boys use their smartphones in Vail, Colorado. (Robert Alexander/Getty Images)

How we did this

Pew Research Center conducted this study to better understand teens’ use of digital devices, social media and other online platforms.

The Center conducted an online survey of 1,391 U.S. teens from Sept. 18 to Oct. 10, 2024, through Ipsos. Ipsos recruited the teens via their parents, who were part of its [KnowledgePanel](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/solutions/public-affairs/knowledgepanel). The KnowledgePanel is a probability-based web panel recruited primarily through national, random sampling of residential addresses. The survey was weighted to be representative of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 who live with their parents by age, gender, race and ethnicity, household income, and other categories.

Here are [the questions used for this report](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_Teens-Social-Media-Tech_TOPLINE.pdf), along with responses, and the [survey methodology](https://www.pewresearch.org/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-tech-methodology/) ­­­.

This research was reviewed and approved by an external institutional review board (IRB), Advarra, an independent committee of experts specializing in helping to protect the rights of research participants.

_For the latest survey data on social media and tech use among teens, see “ [Teens, Social Media and](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/12/09/teens-social-media-and-ai-chatbots-2025/)_ _[AI Chatbots 2025](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/12/09/teens-social-media-and-ai-chatbots-2025/).”_

Amid national concerns about [technology’s impact on youth](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/feature/why-many-parents-and-teens-think-its-harder-being-a-teen-today/), many teens are as digitally connected as ever. Most teens use social media and have a smartphone, and nearly half say they’re online almost constantly, according to a new Pew Research Center survey of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 conducted Sept. 18-Oct. 10, 2024.

[![A line chart showing that YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat top the list for teens](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-01.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195500)

**YouTube tops the list** of the online platforms we asked about in our survey. Nine-in-ten teens report using the site, slightly down from 95% in 2022.

**TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat remain widely used among teens.** Roughly six-in-ten teens say they use TikTok and Instagram, and 55% say the same for Snapchat.

**Facebook and X use have steeply declined over the past decade.** Today, 32% of teens say they use Facebook. This is down from 71% in 2014-15, though the share of teens who use the site has remained stable in recent years. And 17% of teens say they use X (formerly Twitter) – about half the share who said this a decade ago (33%), and down from 23% in 2022.

**Roughly one-quarter of teens (23%) say they use WhatsApp,** up 6 percentage points since 2022.

**And 14% of teens use Reddit,** a share that has remained stable over the past few years.

We asked about **Threads,** [launched by parent company Meta](https://www.cnn.com/2023/07/05/tech/meta-twitter-threads-app-instagram/index.html) in 2023, for the first time this year. Only 6% of teens report using it.

#### More on teens and tech:

- [Cellphones in schools: Most Americans favor class bans, but fewer support all-day bans](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/10/14/most-americans-back-cellphone-bans-during-class-but-fewer-support-all-day-restrictions/)
- [Why Many Parents and Teens Think It’s Harder Being a Teen Today](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/feature/why-many-parents-and-teens-think-its-harder-being-a-teen-today/)

### How often do teens visit online platforms?

[![Circular area charts showing that Similar shares of teens report using TikTok, YouTube, Snapchat and Instagram ‘almost constantly’](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-02.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195501)

Debates about teen social media use often center on how much time teens spend on these platforms. As lawmakers explore potential regulations, our 2023 survey found a majority of Americans [support time limits for minors](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/10/31/81-of-us-adults-versus-46-of-teens-favor-parental-consent-for-minors-to-use-social-media/) on social media.

Our current survey asked teens how often they use five platforms: YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook.

Overall, 73% of teens say they go on YouTube daily, making YouTube the most widely used _and_ visited platform we asked about. This share includes 15% who describe their use as “almost constant.”

About six-in-ten visit TikTok daily. This includes 16% who report being on it almost constantly.

[![A bar chart showing that Roughly three-quarters of teens visit YouTube daily, while around 6 in 10 say this about TikTok](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-03.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195502)

Roughly half of teens say they go on Instagram or Snapchat every day, including about one-in-ten who say they’re on each of these platforms almost constantly.

The share of teens who say they use Instagram almost constantly has increased slightly, from 8% in 2023 to 12% today.

Relatively few teens report using Facebook daily (20%).

Across all five platforms, **one-third of teens use at least one of these sites almost constantly.**

These findings are largely similar to [what we’ve found the past two years](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/12/11/teens-social-media-and-technology-2023/).

#### By gender

[![A dot plot showing that Teen girls are more likely than boys to say they use TikTok almost constantly; the reverse is true for YouTube](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-04.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195503)

As in previous surveys, teen girls are more likely than boys to say they use TikTok almost constantly (19% vs. 13%).

Inversely, teen boys are more likely than girls to use YouTube this often. While 19% of boys say they use it almost constantly, that share drops to 11% among girls.

[Unlike last year](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/12/11/teens-social-media-and-technology-2023/#how-often-do-teens-visit-online-platforms), similar shares of boys (13%) and girls (12%) today say they use Snapchat almost constantly.

There are also no gender differences in the shares of teens who report using Instagram and Facebook almost constantly.

[![A dot plot showing that Roughly a quarter of Black and Hispanic teens report using TikTok, YouTube almost constantly](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-05.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195504)

#### By race and ethnicity

Roughly one-quarter of Black (28%) or Hispanic (25%) teens say they visit TikTok almost constantly. This share drops to 8% among White teens.[1](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/12/12/teens-social-media-and-technology-2024/#fn-195470-1)

Black and Hispanic teens are also more likely than White teens to say they constantly use YouTube or Instagram.

There are few to no racial or ethnic differences in the shares visiting Snapchat and Facebook on a near constant basis.

### How does the use of online platforms differ across demographic groups?

While many teens engage with online platforms, usage varies by gender, race and ethnicity, age, and household income.

[![A table showing that Use of certain online platforms – like Instagram and TikTok – varies by age, race and ethnicity, and gender](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-06.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195505)

#### By gender

Instagram and TikTok are used more widely by teen girls than teen boys. For example, 66% of girls say they use TikTok, compared with 59% of boys. Instagram use follows a similar pattern (66% vs. 56%).

On the other hand, boys are more likely than girls to say they use YouTube (93% vs. 87%).

#### By race and ethnicity

Among teens, a larger share of those who are Black (79%) or Hispanic (74%) than White (54%) say they use TikTok. Black and Hispanic teens also stand out compared with White teens in their use of Instagram and X.

When it comes to the messaging platform WhatsApp, Hispanic teens are more likely than Black or White teens to say they use it.

#### By age

Older teens are more likely than younger teens to use each of the platforms we asked about. Notably, teens ages 15 to 17 are more likely than those ages 13 to 14 say they use Instagram (72% vs. 43%) or Snapchat (63% vs. 44%).

Differences are more modest for platforms like YouTube, which most older (92%) and younger (87%) teens use.

#### By household income

[As was true in prior studies,](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/12/11/teens-social-media-and-technology-2023/#How-use-of-online-platforms-differs-across-demographic-groups) Facebook remains more commonly used among teens in lower-income households. For example, 45% of teens in households earning less than $30,000 a year say they use Facebook. This drops to 35% among teens in households earning $30,000 to $74,999 a year and 29% among teens with household incomes of $75,000 or more.

Teens in lower-income households are more likely than those in the highest-income households to say they use TikTok (73% vs. 59%).

#### By partisanship

Teens who identify as Democrats and Democratic leaners are more likely Republicans and GOP leaners to say they use TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit and WhatApp.

TikTok stands out for its partisan difference: 73% of Democratic teens versus 52% of Republican teens say they use the platform.

[![A bar chart showing Nearly half of teens say they are online ‘almost constantly,’ up from 24% a decade ago](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-07.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195506)

### How much time are teens spending online?

We also asked teens about how often they go online in general.

**Nearly half of teens say they are online almost constantly,** up from 24% a decade ago. This share has stayed consistent over the past few years.

Overall, nearly all teens – 96% – report using the internet daily.

#### By race and ethnicity

[![A bar chart showing that Black, Hispanic teens more likely than White teens to say they use internet almost constantly](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-08.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195507)

Hispanic and Black teens stand out in their screen time. About half or more Hispanic (58%) or Black (53%) teens say they use the internet almost constantly. That share drops to 37% among White teens.

These findings are [consistent with previous Center surveys](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/12/11/teens-social-media-and-technology-2023/#how-much-time-are-teens-spending-online).

#### By age

Being online almost constantly is more common among older teens than younger ones. About half of 15- to 17-year-olds report that they are online this often, compared with 38% of those ages 13 to 14.

### What devices do teens have access to at home?

There’s no one way that today’s teens go online.

[![A bar chart showing that Nearly all teens have access to a smartphone at home](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/12/PI_2024.12.12_teens-social-media-tech_0-09.png)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=195508)

Our latest survey shows that large shares of teens have or have access to a smartphone (95%), desktop or laptop computer (88%), gaming console (83%), or tablet computer (70%) at home.

Overall, smartphone, computer and gaming console ownership has remained stable over the past few years. But the share of teens who say they have access to tablets has risen from 65% in 2023 to 70% today.

#### By age

Most teens say they have or have access to a smartphone. But older teens (98%) are slightly more likely than younger teens (90%) to say this.

Older teens are also more likely than younger teens to have or have access to a desktop or laptop computer (91% vs. 85%).

There are no differences by age when it comes to having a gaming console or tablet computer.

#### By household income

Access to a home computer or a tablet is most common among teens in high-income households.

- **Desktop or laptop computer:** 93% of teens living in households whose annual income is $75,000 or more have access to a home computer. That share falls to about eight-in-ten among those whose annual household income is $30,000 to $74,999 (81%) or less than $30,000 (78%).
- **Tablet computer:** About three-quarters of teens whose annual household income is $75,000 or more (73%) have access to a tablet at home, compared with 64% each among teens whose annual household income is $30,000 to $74,999 and those whose household income is less than $30,000.

#### By gender

**Majorities of boys and girls have access to a** **gaming console, but boys stand out.** Nine-in-ten teenage boys say they have access to a gaming console at home, while about three quarters of girls say this (76%).

For more on gender differences in video game use, read our 2023 report: [Teens and Video Games Today](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/05/09/teens-and-video-games-today/).
