# Brainrot Slang Explained: The Ultimate Guide to Gen Z & Gen Alpha Brainrot Words (With A–Z Glossary + Examples)

[Elly Kim](https://promova.com/author/elly-kim)reviewed by [Olena Grabova](https://promova.com/expert/olena-grabova) / [more about Editorial Process](https://promova.com/our-editorial-process)23min

Last updated: Jul 31, 2026

![Brainrot Slang](https://promova.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpromova.com%2Fcontent%2Fbrainrot_slang_e95088d9a2.png&w=3840&q=75)

[English Slang](https://promova.com/blog?tag=english-slang)

ExplanationFlashcards

## Contents

## Key takeaways:

> - Brainrot slang is fast, meme-driven internet language that spreads mainly on TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Discord, and gaming spaces.
> - A brain rot words list helps you decode viral terms like _rizz, skibidi,_ and _sigma_ without guessing.
> - Meanings can change overnight, so context (platform + tone + trend) matters more than “dictionary rules.”
> - Brainrot slang is often ironic and self-aware — the chaos is part of the joke.
> - Learning a few core brainrot words can help you understand memes, comments, and group chats in modern English.

Spend a few minutes on TikTok or YouTube Shorts, and you might feel like you’ve entered another dimension. One where nonsense words like “skibidi,” “rizz,” and “sigma” are tossed around as if they were perfectly normal English words. These are often called 'rot words'—a shorthand for the viral, absurd, and meme-driven internet slang that dominates digital conversations.

Welcome to the world of brainrot slang! This chaotic, ever-evolving digital dialect—also known as rot words—was born from the meme culture and the hyper-digital lives of Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Brainrot words refer to internet slang and nonsensical phrases popular among these generations, originating from excessive, low-quality content consumption on social media. These words often stem from constant exposure to low-value online content on platforms like TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Discord.

The cultural shift is clear: 'tiktok brain' and digital culture have accelerated the spread and evolution of brainrot slang, making it a defining feature of how young people communicate online. Notably, 'brain rot' was named the 2024 Word of the Year by Oxford University Press.

In this article, we’ll decode what brainrot is, the most popular brainrot slang meanings, and show you how to use brainrot slang naturally, so you can finally keep up with kids.

## **The origin of brainrot**

Brainrot, or is it brain rot? And is it some kind of disease you should be worried about? If you’ve ever asked yourself these questions, you’re not alone, and you’re in the right place.

Let’s start with the basics. Brain rot (or brainrot) isn’t a medical condition. It’s a viral slang term that’s taken over the internet and was even voted as the [2024 Oxford word of the year](https://corp.oup.com/news/brain-rot-named-oxford-word-of-the-year-2024/).

Let’s start with the basics. Brain rot (or brainrot) is a viral internet slang term used to describe the feeling of mental overload or “mush brain” after consuming too much fast, low-effort online content. The term became so widespread that it was named the 2024 Word of the Year by Oxford University Press, which defines it more formally as the “mental deterioration caused by overconsumption of trivial or unchallenging content.”

But what does it mean? And where has it come from? Read on to find out.

**The beginning**

It might surprise you that “brain rot” is not a modern invention. The phrase dates back to 1854, when Henry David Thoreau used it in his book _Walden_. Thoreau used the term to criticize what he felt was society’s preference to value simple ideas over complex ones, and felt it was an indication of the general decline in the general public’s mental and intellectual efforts.

**Before the memes**

Before it became internet slang, “brain rot” was used by parents, teachers, and older generations to describe content that they perceived as intellectually unstimulating. Think reality TV, video games, and trashy talk shows that would “rot your brain.” The term "video game" in particular became a frequent target, as gaming culture and viral video game references started to influence online slang and meme trends. This connection helped set the stage for brainrot slang to evolve alongside internet memes and gaming communities.

**Internet humor takes over**

As meme culture exploded and social media evolved, the phrase took on a new life online. Reddit, Tumblr, and early TikTok users began using “brainrot” as a tongue-in-cheek way of describing their own scrolling habits, not as a warning but as a punchline. A way to describe that feeling of your brain turning to mush after endlessly doomscrolling and watching short, mentally unstimulating videos. Brainrot words often serve as inside jokes or viral reactions within online communities, making them difficult for outsiders to understand.

**Brainrot goes viral (2021-2023)**

When platforms like TikTok and Discord exploded on the scene, the use of brainrot skyrocketed. The hyper-digital Gen Z and Gen Alpha began creating and consuming nonsensical, fast-paced, short-form videos, and “brainrot” evolved to describe:

- The state of mind after bingeing on content. For example: “ _This video gave me brainrot and I loved it.”_
- A genre of absurd, nonsensical humor that thrives on randomness. For example, Italian brainrot.
- A type of slang that often makes no sense but is instantly recognizable to those “in the know.” For example, “Skibidi,” “rizz,” and “Ohio.”

**Today (2025)**

“Brain rot” has become more than just a phrase; it’s become a culture, a vibe, and a language. Whether it’s the way people talk or the content they consume, brainrot reflects a cultural shift in how the younger generations communicate and the online identities they’re forming. Brainrot now acts as generational shorthand, fostering community among Gen Alpha and Gen Z while creating communication gaps with older adults.

Ever-evolving, this kind of ironic, often self-deprecating humor doesn’t always make sense, but for the younger generations, it doesn’t have to.

## Gen Z Brainrot Slang List: A-to-Z Slang Glossary

**A**

[**Aura farming**](https://www.tiktok.com/@greenscreens4memes/video/7521969406323281157?q=Aura%20farming&t=1752917576524) **:** Refers to someone constantly trying to look cool or build “aura moments”.

- **Origin:** Derived from brainrot slang “aura,” which refers to someone’s vibe or energy.
- **Context:** Can be used negatively to call people out or positively when trying to emulate someone else’s positive aura.
- **Example:** “Did you see the video of the kid dancing on the front of the boat? He’s the ultimate aura farmer.”

**B**

[**Beige flag**](https://www.tiktok.com/@matt.and.aves/video/7478912019425463607?lang=en) **:** A quirk in someone’s personality that’s neither positive nor negative but still gives you pause.

- **Origin:** TikTok, 2023.
- **Context:** Meant as funny or self-deprecating, not negative like ‘red flags’.
- **Example:** “His beige flag is that he claps when the plane lands.”

[**Bussin**](https://www.tiktok.com/@bussinsnacks) **:** Really good, usually in reference to food.

- **Origin:** Popularized in 2020 by the “gripping food with force” trend.
- **Context:** Can be used genuinely or ironically.
- **Example:** “This sushi is bussin”

[**Brat**](https://www.tiktok.com/@brat365xcx/video/7500402845909355807?q=Brat%20girl%20summer&t=1752916963254) **:** A girl enjoying life to the max, speaking their mind, or having a demanding or playfully difficult attitude.

- **Origin:** Popularized by Charli XCX’s new album
- **Context:** Usually used in a positive context to highlight confidence, boldness, or rebelliousness.
- **Example:** “She’s giving brat energy today.”

**C**

[**Cap (no cap)**](https://www.tiktok.com/@englishwithtiffani/video/7307249141120306438) **:**“Cap” = lie, “No cap” = telling the truth.

- **Origin:** popularized in 2017 in the Atlanta hip-hop scene, but has been used in rap music since the mid-1980s.
- **Context:** Used to reinforce that you are not lying or being in disbelief, like saying “no way.”
- **Example:** “That fit is fire, no cap.”

**D**

[**Delulu**](https://www.tiktok.com/@muricanmike/video/7349234106674236680?q=Delulu&t=1752918336387) **:** Slang for “delusional” used playfully to justify

- **Origin:** Shortened from delusional on Stan Twitter and K-pop fan spaces.
- **Context:** Usually used as a jokey description of yourself.
- **Example:** “We made eye contact, so that means we’re basically dating. I’m delulu.”

**E**

[**Eboy/Egirl**](https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/e-girl-e-boy) **:** A subcultural ‘look’ that blends emo, alt, and anime fashion.

- **Origin:** Evolved from emo and scene subcultures, popularized via early TikTok.
- **Context:** A visual identity rather than just a personality; associated with alternative fashion, exaggerated poses, and curated edginess.
- **Example:** “He’s a total Eboy. Black nail polish, chains, and TikTok thirst traps.”

**F**

[**FYP**](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/FYP) **:** TikTok’s “For You Page,” your main feed.

- **Origin:** TikTok feature name.
- **Context:** Used when something is trending hard.
- **Example:** “This sound is all over my FYP.”

**G**

[**Gyatt**](https://www.tiktok.com/@tatakiii/video/7286120636961885473?lang=en) **:** A loud, exaggerated exclamation meaning “goddamn” or used to refer to a person’s posterior.

- **Origin:** Popularized by Twitch streamers YourRage and Kai Cenat.
- **Context:** Used humorously, often in reaction content, especially by streamers.
- **Example:** “GYATT, did you see that girl walk by?”

[**Goblin mode**](https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-63857329) **:** Indulging in messy, lazy behavior without shame.

- **Origin:** Exploded in the early 2020s and became the Oxford Word of the Year 2022.
- **Context:** Used without shame and even as a form of self-care, where you shake off societal norms about how you look.
- **Example:** “I haven’t left the house in days—I’m in full goblin mode”

**H**

[**Heather**](https://www.tiktok.com/@marlonhafid._/video/7522623527225232645?q=Heather&t=1752920116640) **:** A girl who everyone likes, she’s effortlessly cool, attractive, and someone others admire but like.

- **Origin:** Comes from Conan Gray’s 2020 song “heather”.
- **Context:** Gen Z turned it into a cultural label for someone unintentionally popular or stylish. It can be used genuinely or ironically.
- **Example:** “I wish I was Heather”

**I**

[**Ick**](https://www.tiktok.com/@wyszkay/video/7337087459026636064?q=Ick&t=1752920413809) **:** Something that makes you feel uncomfortable or turned off by a person or a situation.

- **Origin:** The Ally McBeal TV show in 1998.
- **Context:** Can be used negatively to describe actions that have put you off someone romantically or sexually. Also used in a humorous way to make fun of a partner's “quirks.”
- **Example:** “Ugh, sandals with socks. Ick.”

**J**

[**Jump scare**](https://www.tiktok.com/@shumibrody/video/7185633192248888622) **:** A sudden, shocking reveal. Usually, it’s about someone’s appearance, an old photo, or a messy situation.

- **Origin:** Borrowed from horror films and recontextualized by Gen Z.
- **Context:** Used for humor or self-roasting.
- **Example:**“I just saw my middle school yearbook photo…jump scare.”

**K**

[**Karen**](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-53588201) **:** A derogatory term to describe an entitled, demanding, often white woman who uses her privilege to police others.

- **Origin:** Exploded in 2020 amid viral videos of a white woman calling police on people of color.
- **Context:** It has become shorthand for privilege, entitlement, and passive-aggressive behavior. Some argue it is a sexist and outdated term; however, it is a relevant social archetype description.
- **Example:** “Not her asking for the manager again… Karen.”

**L**

[**Let him cook**](https://www.tiktok.com/@championsleague/video/7199981015052422406?q=Let%20him%20cook&t=1752921801397) **:** A phrase used when someone is doing something questionable, but you want to give them a chance, or someone is doing something really well and you want them to continue.

- **Origin:** From sports commentary and Black Twitter, it went viral on TikTok in 2022.
- **Context:** Can be used sincerely and sarcastically.
- **Example:** “I don’t know what he’s doing, but let him cook.”

**M**

[**Mewing**](https://www.tiktok.com/@calgenius/video/7424673528701619487?q=Mewing&t=1752922144984) **:** A technique of placing your tongue on the roof of your mouth that supposedly improves jawline and facial structure over time.

- **Origin:** Coined by Dr John Mew, a British orthodontist.
- **Context:** Used as a “looksmaxxing” trend, not as a medical practice. Some use it seriously, some as humor. It also has links to incel and manosphere circles, but it’s more often used in mainstream meme humor.
- **Example:** “I’ve been mewing for 6 months now; can you tell?”

**N**

[**NPC**](https://www.reddit.com/r/OutOfTheLoop/comments/11vyf5f/what_is_up_with_the_abbreviations_npc/) **(Non-player character):** An insult or meme describing someone who doesn’t think for themselves.

- **Origin:** From the gaming culture. NPCs are background characters in video games.
- **Context:** Used as a derogatory term to describe people who follow social scripts, lack originality, or repeat opinions.
- **Example:** “She’s so basic, literally an NPC.”

**O**

[**Ohio**](https://www.tiktok.com/@goofy.pollo/video/7450226932643335446?q=Ohio&t=1752923030093) **(“only in Ohio”, “What’s going on in Ohio”):** Several different meme phrases used to describe something as “weird” or “bizarre.”

- **Origin:** Originating from crazy videos and news articles coming out of Ohio.
- **Context:** Used by Gen Alpha and zoomers to describe something as weird.
- **Example:** “Our substitute teacher started beatboxing and challenged us to a rap battle.”

“What kind of Ohio school is this?”

[**Pick me**](https://www.tiktok.com/@realburnttoasthehe/video/7482873515415293226?q=Pick%20me%20girl&t=1752923574566) **:** Someone (often a girl) who seeks male approval by putting others down or performing for male attention.

- **Origin:** Twitter and TikTok, circa 2019-2020
- **Context:** Can be used as an insult or as self-deprecating humor. It’s now expanded to “pick me boys”.
- **Example:**“She said ‘I’m not like other girls’, classic pick me energy.”

**R**

[**Rizz**](https://www.tiktok.com/@fallontonight/video/7478563548642168106?lang=en) **:** Short for ‘charisma.’ It means charisma, presence, or game, especially in the context of flirting.

- **Origin:** Popularized by influencer Kai Cenat.
- **Context:** “Unspoken rizz” means someone who is not even trying but has charisma.
- **Example:** “She used her rizz to get free drinks.”

**S**

[**Skibidi**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WePNs-G7puA) **:** A nonsensical catchphrase turned meme. Most commonly associated with chaotic, surreal YouTube shorts videos featuring characters like “skibidi toilet”.

- **Origin:** First gained attention in 2018 in the song “skibidi” by Little Big, a Russian rave band. However, it exploded in 2023 with the brainrot trend “skibidi toilet.”
- **Context:** It’s peak Gen Alpha brain rot.
- **Example:**“When the beat drops, it’s Skibidi o’clock.”

[**Sigma**](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/UHm7NJCyC48) **:** A term used to describe a “lone wolf” type of male. They typically reject societal norms and don’t crave validation, but are (or at least think they are) successful.

- **Origin:** Coined in online manosphere spaces as an alternative to the Alpha/Beta male hierarchy. Gained momentum in 2020-2022.
- **Context:** Originally used as a serious description in red-pill spaces, it’s now been satirized by Gen Z. Some use it seriously, others as a way to make fun of hustle-culture, incels, and those in the Andrew Tate space.
- **Example:** “Sigma males don’t chase; they attract.”

**T**

[**Touch grass**](https://www.tiktok.com/tag/touchgrass) **:** A dismissive way of telling someone they've spent way too much time online and need to go outside. According to Game Quitters' brainrot slang glossary, it's one of the most common put-downs for extremely online behavior.

- **Origin:** Popularized on Reddit and 4chan before spreading to TikTok and Twitter/X.
- **Context:** Used to mock someone who's overreacting online or arguing over something trivial.
- **Example:** “You're mad about a video game character's outfit? Touch grass.”

**U**

[**Unc**](https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/unc) **:** Short for “uncle,” used to poke fun at someone (usually a peer) acting old-fashioned, out of touch, or overly cautious.

- **Origin:** African American Vernacular English, popularized further through TikTok and gaming Discords.
- **Context:** Often teasing, not meant as a real insult about age.
- **Example:** “Bro said he doesn't trust apps with Face ID… unc behavior.”

**V**

[**Vibe check**](https://www.tiktok.com/@sarabirganii/video/7429750022473878816?q=Vibe%20check&t=1752924839138) **:** A test of someone’s vibe or energy.

- **Origin:** Tumblr and X circa 2019
- **Context:** Can be playful or mean-spirited.
- **Example:**“He failed the vibe check when he told me he listened to Coldplay.”

**W**

[**Womp womp**](https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/womp-womp) **:** A sarcastic sound effect (like a sad trombone) said or typed after someone shares bad news or a weak excuse, showing mock sympathy or dismissal.

- **Origin:** Comes from the classic “sad trombone” sound effect, adopted into text form on TikTok and Discord.
- **Context:** Often used bluntly to shut down complaints, sometimes affectionately among friends.
- **Example:** “I forgot my charger and my phone died.” “Womp womp.”

**Y**

[**Yapping**](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/yapping) **:** Talking too much (often teasing).

- **Origin:** TikTok slang, later widely used on Discord.
- **Context:** Used jokingly or lightly teasing someone who talks a lot or goes off-topic.
- **Example:** “Bro keeps yapping, get to the point.”

**Z**

[**Zesty**](https://www.tiktok.com/@smoothgioofficial/video/7444695550793944366?lang=en) **:** Slang for someone flamboyant, expressive, or “too much.”

- **Origin:** Black slang, later picked up by Stan and meme culture.
- **Context:** Can be used to mock or flatter depending on tone.
- **Example:**“His roast was extra zesty, no cap.”

### What is brainrot slang for?

Brainrot slang is an online language born from meme culture, online gaming forums, and other popular platforms. Generally created by Gen Z and Gen Alpha, these slang terms can go viral overnight, suddenly being the “it” thing to say or post about. But, like with most things “viral,” they can also disappear just as quickly as they arrived.

### What are examples of brainrot words slang?

Ever heard of the likes of Skibidi, rizz, Gyatt, Ohio, or bussin? Nope, then you must be delulu.

### What does brainrot mean in a meme?

Brainrot refers to the absurd, low-quality, and chaotic content often found online on platforms like TikTok and YouTube Shorts. While it’s usually meant to be funny, people call it “brainrot” as a tongue-in-cheek way of saying that this kind of mindless entertainment is slowly “rotting their brain.”

### Where did brainrot slang originate?

Brainrot slang has originated online among the younger generations. It’s not only used as a form of communication but also as a signal that you’re highly digitally connected and “in the know.” Often born from viral memes, this bizarre and chaotic language evolves quickly and often makes no sense, and that’s part of the fun.

## The Ultimate Glossary of TikTok Slang for 2025

Remember when “cool beans” was the height of slang?

Cute.

Fast forward to 2025, and we’re drowning in a sea of TikTok slang where new phrases flood in faster than we can say, “Wait, _what’s_ a skibidi toilet?”

Whether you’re a parent deciphering what your kid meant by “Ohio” at the dinner table or a marketer keen on not sounding like Steve Buscemi when advertising to Generation Z or Generation Alpha, you’re in the right place.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792d0c3a238d8200946bdcc_679287d71e433a7b73bfa843_steve.png)

Below is the ultimate glossary of top TikTok slang words used in 2025 (and beyond). After reading, you won’t just have an expanded vocabulary to better connect with TikTok’s [1.5 billion users](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/tiktok-stats/); you’ll know how to create native and relatable campaigns—positioning your brand at the center of the conversation…and not the punchline.

Period. 🫰

## The Glossary of TikTok Slang in 2025

## Alpha

Gen Z uses “alpha” to describe a **dominant, powerful, and hyper-masculine man**. While some see the word as a compliment and aspiration, others consider it the result of toxic masculinity.

**Example**:

> “I only date alpha males—someone who is financially independent and the leader of his friend group.”

‍

## Altered My Brain Chemistry

With over [53.7M views](https://www.tiktok.com/tag/alteredbrainchemistry?lang=en) and counting, the #alteredmybrainchemistry trend shows no sign of slowing down. On TikTok, saying that something “altered your brain chemistry” is to say that it was **such a powerful moment or memory that it changed you as a person**.

Of course, being TikTok, it’s not as serious as it sounds. Many of the examples from this trend are nonchalant or are to make others laugh.

**‍** [**Example**](https://www.tiktok.com/@louiethecream/video/7168655834875104558?is_copy_url=1&is_from_webapp=v1&lang=en) **:**

> _“Moment with my dog that altered my brain chemistry: when he got stung by a bee.”  🐝_ ‍

‍

## Aura Points

If you don’t know what aura points are, you just lost 100 of them. (Kidding.) “ [Aura points](https://www.tiktok.com/@mr_lindsay_sped/video/7379390300281654571?lang=en)” **measure your coolness or charisma**, and certain actions can either **boost** or **drop** your score.

**Example:**

> “How many aura points did I lose when I waved back at someone saying hi only to realize they weren’t waving at me?”

‍

## Beige flag

A “beige flag" is **a romantic partner’s weird or peculiar trait**. It’s neither good or bad (i.e. not a green nor a red flag), but it is telling of someone's personality.

**Example:**

> “My husband's [beige flag](https://www.tiktok.com/@embern/video/7329622597019258142?lang=en&q=beige%20flag&t=1735326599105) is that he sets an alarm on his phone to remind him to eat his cookie at 9:30 PM.”

‍

## Beta

If an “alpha” is the leader of the pack, the “beta” is the runt of the litter. The term refers to someone **subservient, insecure, and weak**—and it’s (unsurprisingly) used as an insult.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“She cheated on him three times and he keeps taking her back. He’s such a beta._”

‍

## BDE

BDE is an abbreviation for **Big Dick Energy**. This is slang to describe **someone or something that is confident, aspirational, and powerful** (and it isn’t necessarily reserved just for men). That’s because BDE is an emotional/psychological attribute - not a physical attribute.

‍

**Example:**

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa5d9091c5bb137f1ec_qBF2bHUS7ZNkzIwIyGiu-J_WWoH9pVPgka-nTYydczsr9z86448hnEMotFGuGxi3JSNdtHGAPWaBa-6WbkkhiKk65MIO5w3RZl88LtR2l3wOaMKj7aE-Fk27qFAoR8bVPK_5z9QwEeUbI1bLqJBbDkC27ekRXOlScTox0KY2IB20fkLsP_gGz_D4ZYO5ug.png)

## Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL)

You’ll find _lots_ of videos on TikTok showing the “before and after” of a cosmetic procedure and the Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL) is no exception. **The BBL is a popular surgery where a surgeon places fat from one area of the body to the 🍑 make it appear larger.** Accounts often post their “BBL” results on TikTok.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“I traveled to Mexico to get a BBL and here are the results!”_ ‍

‍

## Be so for real

“Be so for real” is a **playful yet pointed way to call out a moment that feels unbelievable or over-the-top**. It’s the modern-day equivalent of “Are you serious?” or “Don’t play with me.”

**Example:**

> “My 12-year-old sister told her friends she would never trust boys again after her ex dumped her. Like girl. Be so for real.”

‍

## Bones Day or No Bones Day

The “Bones” or “No Bones” day saying came from Noodle, an elderly pug on TikTok, and his owner Jonathan Graziano. Graziano would help Noodle stand in his dog bed and if Noodle stayed up, it was a **“bones day” — meaning a good day to go and be productive.** But if Noodle sank back into his bed, it was a “ **no bones” day: a signal to go and take it easy**.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“Noodle said it was a no bones day, so I’m not doing anything today.”_ ‍

‍

## Brain rot

Coined [Oxford’s Word of the Year 2024](https://corp.oup.com/news/brain-rot-named-oxford-word-of-the-year-2024/), “brain rot” describes **the deterioration of one’s mental state after consuming low-quality content online**. In other words? “Brain rot” is that zoned-out feeling you get after bingeing on bizarre videos, silly memes, petty online drama, and pointless quizzes (e.g. “What Type of Bread Are You?”).

‍

**Example**:

> “My Instagram is brain rot lately. I feel dumber after scrolling after five minutes.”

‍

## Brat

The title of pop singer Charli XCX’s studio album, “ [brat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brat_(album)#:~:text=Brat%20is%20the%20sixth%20studio,partner%20George%20Daniel%2C%20and%20others.)” isn’t just a noun or adjective: It’s a cultural phenomenon. [Charli XCX](https://www.tiktok.com/@charlixcx/video/7386786386298342688?is_from_webapp=1&web_id=7326907923145197099) describes “brat” as:

“Someone who has a pack of cigs, a Bic lighter, and a strappy white top with no bra. You’re just like a girl who is a little messy and likes to party…is very honest, very blunt. A little bit volatile.”

Charli XCX’s "brat" is **the grown-up rendition of the “bratty” petulant child**—now a fearless adult who embraces nonconformity and youthful defiance.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/67928a31926b4c507121ecfa_ab047e16-f100-4428-af46-848f867c454c.png)

**Example:** ‍

> “It was the middle of July and all the girls were strutting through Manhattan with wraparound Y2K sunglasses, wired headphones, and a mild hangover. It was peak brat summer.”

‍

## Cap

If someone **says “cap” or uses the cap emoji (🧢) on TikTok they’re saying it’s a lie**. Conversely, “no cap” means they’re telling the truth.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“No cap, I was able to get tickets to Taylor Swift’s tour.”_ ‍

‍

## CEO (of Something)

A CEO (Chief Executive Officer) is defined as the highest-ranking person in an organization and handles major decisions. But if you’re called a CEO on TikTok, it means **you’re the leader or most talented** at something — and usually it's a random and trivial field.

Used in another sense, referring to the CEO of something can be a play on the Karen meme. In this usage, someone is facetiously saying that want to speak to the CEO (i.e., whoever is in charge) of something - usually an abstract concept. This is a way of expressing that you have an issue with the concept/thing in question.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“You used blueberry goat cheese and prosciutto?! You’re the CEO of charcuterie boards.”_

> "I would like to speak to the CEO of ADHD, I cannot get anything done today!"

‍

## Chat

“Chat” isn’t those friendly conversations you have by the water cooler. Here, “chat” **refers to a fourth person**, similar to “guys” or “everyone.” It originated from streamers on [Twitch](https://www.tiktok.com/@hitzdotmy/video/7390332789540932872?lang=en) who used the term to address their live audience in the [chat](https://help.twitch.tv/s/article/chat-basics?language=en_US) window.

‍ **Example:**

> **‍**“Chat, should I pick the blue or red outfit for tonight’s stream?”

‍

## Coconut tree

In May 2023, Vice President Kamala Harris dropped a memorable (and bizarre) line [during a speech](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JWR29RT5sw) on education equity: “You think you just fell out of a coconut tree?”

Fast forward to her presidential campaign, and the one-liner returned in full force. The phrase became **an ironic slogan for her campaign**—with supporters dubbing her run “Operation Coconut Tree” and flooding social media with coconut emojis. 🥥

**Example:**

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792bc38d017a93d6cf8ecc6_2691a198-b4ff-4a5b-ba02-da0841c3893f.png)

‍

## Coded

“Coded” **refers to someone or something that embodies specific traits**. If you’re “millennial coded,” that means you have the stereotypical characteristics of a millennial, such as a love for avocado toast and skinny jeans.

**Example**:

> “He responded to my Instagram story with a laughing crying emoji. He’s so millennial coded.”

‍

## Cooked

If someone is “cooked,” it means **they’re exhausted, in trouble, or under the influence**.  It can be used in the same way a "screwed," but also has a broader range.

**Example:**

> “I can’t go to your party tonight. I know it'll be fun but I just got home from a 12-hour shift. I’m cooked.”

‍

## Cheugy

If someone calls you Cheugy, you might want to revisit your life choices. Kidding, but this is a word to describe **someone (or something) that’s not quite uncool, but not exactly cool, either**. It’s a middle ground of cringe — something that’s just _slightly_ out of touch.

It can be a font, the “girl boss” energy, the Applebees in Times Square, Santacon in NYC, and Minions. But, one thing is certain: nothing is safe from being considered “cheugy.”

**Example:** ‍

> ‍ _“She had one of those ‘Live Laugh Love’ signs in her bathroom and it was so cheugy.”_ ‍

‍

## Dead (or 💀 )

If you see someone saying “dead” on TikTok that doesn’t actually mean they’re dead. For Gen-Z, "dead" or the skull emoji, **means that something was so funny that they died laughing**. This slang has begun to replace the typical laughing face emoji  (😂) with the skull emoji (💀) to signal laughter.

**Example:**

> _“Wait, did you see that funny video I sent you on TikTok? I’m dead.”_ ‍

‍

## Delulu

“Delulu” is an abbreviation for ‘delusional’ and **describes someone unreasonably optimistic or out of touch with reality**.

**Example:**

> “When I was 13 years old I went to a Justin Bieber concert and thought he’d notice me in the crowd. I was delulu.”

‍

## Demure

Being “demure” is about **being mindful, subtle, and not doing too much**. The term went viral after creator [Jools Lebron](https://www.tiktok.com/@joolieannie/video/7398612571818888494) posted a TikTok showing how she comes to work:

“I do my makeup. I lay my wig. I flat iron my hair. Very demure, very mindful. Let’s not forget to be demure, divas.”

There's a way to be “demure” in almost any situation—from [exiting a plane](https://www.tiktok.com/@joolieannie/video/7402416445969239338) to [thanking hotel staff](https://www.tiktok.com/@joolieannie/video/7402329514249932074) to even [applying baby oil](https://www.tiktok.com/@joolieannie/video/7416471982125878570).

**Example**:

> “See how I leave the bathroom after taking a shower? No clothes on the floor. No water spilled everywhere. Skincare on. Very demure, very mindful.”

‍

## For the plot

Coined by TikToker [Serena Kerrigan](https://www.tiktok.com/@serenakerrigan/video/7122172983526821163?q=Serena%20kerrigan%20do%20it%20for%20the%20plot&t=1704108696298), “for the plot” **means to do bold (and sometimes absurd) things to add spice and spontaneity to your life**.

‍ **Example:**

> “He’s unemployed and just got out of prison but of course I’m still going to go on a date with him. It's for the plot.”

‍

## E-Girl (or Egirl)

With nearly [**25 billion views**](https://www.tiktok.com/tag/egirl?lang=en) **,** the e-girl (electronic girl) is a quintessential trope in the world of TikTok. According to Vox reporter [Rebecca Jennings](https://www.vox.com/the-goods/2019/8/1/20748707/egirl-definition-what-is-an-eboy), an e-girl is a “category of hip young people whose defining qualities are that they are hot and online.”

But unlike the classic Kardashian influencers that you can find in the wild, the e-girl seldom leaves her room. She sports pigtails, crop tops, colorful hair clips, purple hair, knee-high stockings or schoolgirl skirts — it's a sort of neologism of an aesthetic, blending elements of early 2000s "scene," adolescent fashion, and it's own spin.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“I’m sick of partying. I’m going to get into gaming, stay in my room, and just become an e-girl instead.”_

‍

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa6fbb2db99fad400df_CYEGoy6-3rGzneRl07j6oijUKp1Q7nYfp5u9ago0d7AxcZJUbyqwzkeOEgtj4A-Mo71FLiY4lmEKsXliVMWwnzV2AF33IgOW80MuLhnU7SAXpOyQtUmv1i3RAO9YejolFQ-z-Se-KadVbKSuJbDP-I6YKYmJPBZRqN5651pT73BWil39H3qRcr-sYtR3Iw.jpeg)

‍

## Fit

On TikTok, “fit” is **slang for outfit** and is used to describe one’s choice of clothing. However, British people will also say “fit” to describe someone as attractive (so just pay attention to the accent the word is said in 😉).

**Example:**

> ‍ _“So for the fit today we have a coach bag, dress from Princess Polly, and shoes from Doc Martens.”_ ‍

‍

## Fridgescaping

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792bd78383b838e79f4971e_c8ffc3fe-8add-49fe-a623-994362b11574.png)

“Fridgescaping” is **the art of decorating your refrigerator’s interior**. It goes beyond organizing food—people will put flowers, sculptures, and even fairy lights all in the name of enhancing their fridge's aesthetic.

Some even design full-blown themes, from festive [Christmas Carol](https://www.tiktok.com/@lynziliving/video/7434664685032574239) displays to [Bridgerton-inspired](https://www.tiktok.com/@lynziliving/video/7381605725727952158) setups (aptly named “Fridgerton.”)

**Example**:

> “Gina’s fridgescaping skills are awesome. She did a Halloween theme and had skulls, cobwebs, and plastic spiders in her fridge.”

‍

## Fire (🔥) or Lit

If something is awesome or cool, people will describe it as “lit” or “fire.” It’s not uncommon to see people just use the fire emoji (🔥) as well to communicate this. This slang can be used to describe almost anything, from clothes, to apartments, to celebrations, or food.

Example:

> “ _We went to Nobu for his 45th birthday and it was so fire.”_ ‍

‍

## Girl math

“Girl math” describes how people (especially young women) **use creative logical maneuvers to rationalize their purchases**.

In [girl math world](https://mashable.com/article/what-is-girl-math-explained), cash isn’t “real” money. A loaded Starbucks app means free coffee. Botox counts as an investment. And if you _don’t_ buy something when it’s on sale? You’re actually losing money.

**Example**:

> “I bought this $300 coat but it’s reversible, so it’s two coats in one. And if I wear the coat 50 times this winter that’s only $6 per wear! Girl math.”

‍

## GYAT or GYAAT

This is the **abbreviation for “Get Your Act Together,”** is used in the context of when **you’re discreetly appreciating someone’s body shape - it is a way of admonishing oneself**. First popularized by streamer YourRAGE to refer to whenever someone curvy popped up on his streams, consider it another alternative to “damnnnn.”

**Example:**

‍

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa51a1b2cb3479bbfd6_ZNWPFq1ZozPK3MwDggzo0MN3rcw95L-IsYnXMrDwcJBEML-R7dVRIu5trFoXSOiuTAOIzDuyg3T0cXW56SYt2O3F525MzAU1BARkO74wG5ddezFb74hqEZNfGdafK3Pls3AG6V1eAdUpMSaR9mmLJIYqAwSJPdzeueXnHmJs56iYdMadPZ8UybR0OWsZ_A.png)

## Heather

The slang word “Heather” was inspired by Conan Gray’s song, where he describes the familiar gut-wrenching scenario of your crush being in love with the popular and pretty “Heather” instead. Essentially, a “ **Heather” is _the_“it girl” — it’s who everyone wants to be and is in love with**.

Having a “Heather” in your life is a universal feeling many TikTokers can relate to, with one “Heather” TikTok accumulating over 175K likes and hundreds of comments.

**‍** [**Example**](https://www.tiktok.com/@sophiaanastasiaa/video/6865334243761917190?embed_source=70846777%2C120811592%2C120810756%3Bnull%3Bembed_masking&is_copy_url=1&is_from_webapp=v1&refer=embed&referer_url=www.popbuzz.com%2F&referer_video_id=6865334243761917190) **:**

> ‍ _“My mom was such a heather in high school.”_ ‍

‍

## Holding space

Psychologist Marie Bobby [defines](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/11/25/a-psychologist-explains-what-holding-space-actually-means.html) “holding space” as “ **creating a safe, compassionate environment** where someone can feel seen, heard, and understood without judgment or interruption.”

**Example**:

> “My girlfriend is amazing at holding space for me after a long day at my 9–5. I’ll have the longest rants but she never judges me.”

‍

## Hawk tuah

The Hawk Tuah phenomenon began when 21-year-old Hailey Welch was stopped on the street for a [TikTok interview](https://www.tiktok.com/@videoman_byahpositive/video/7383483959180643617?lang=en) and asked to share a move that “ **drives a man crazy in bed**.”

Her response? “You gotta give ‘em that ‘hawk tuah’ and spit on that thang!” referring to the act of giving oral sex. Her brazen reply went viral, generating over 27 million views and 571,900 likes on TikTok–and [Hawk Tuah](https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/story/the-hawk-tuah-girl-everything-you-need-and-absolutely-dont-need-to-know#:~:text=Caption%20Options&text=Welch's%20response?,Hawk%20Tuah%20Girl%20was%20born.) girl was born.

**Example**:

> “If she don’t hawk tuah I won’t talk tuah.”

‍

## Ick

According to Urban Dictionary, the "ick" is that **feeling of mild disgust when you see a prospective romantic partner doing something embarrassing or gross**.

**Example**:

> “That guy I was dating? I have zero desire to see him again. He gave me the ick when he told me he hadn’t gone to the dentist in 10 years. What is wrong with him?”

‍

## It’s Giving

“It’s giving” is used to describe the **vibe that thing brings.** TikTok’s fashion communities usually say it to describe the look of an outfit, but can also be used as a way to say someone or something is exceptional (i.e. “it’s serving”).

**Example:**

> ‍ _“So I put on this apron as a fashion statement, but it’s giving Denny’s waitress.”_

‍

## In da clerb we all fam

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792c71287d9aa55fbbd0508_d1927d47-e297-43a2-bd50-1e91e7135990.jpeg)

Does “In da clerb we all fam” sound vaguely familiar? That’s because it’s from a [2016 episode](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=umvJQXZlSHw) of the hit TV sitcom _Broad City_ starring Ilana Glazer and Abbi Jacobson.

The video shows Illana waving to strangers at the club. “Do you know them?” asks Abbi. “No,” replies Illana. “But in da clerb we all fam.”

The clip regained popularity after comedian [Maggie Winters](https://www.tiktok.com/@saggiesplinters) posted it on TikTok. It wasn’t long before people started using “In da clerb we all fam” to describe that **certain situation when strangers feel like family**—whether it’s at a [hibachi dinner](https://www.tiktok.com/@rach.neeldeman/video/7424655730432609567?is_from_webapp=1&web_id=7293202018252113450) or in [church](https://www.tiktok.com/@shelby.alysa/video/7422743584648105262?is_from_webapp=1&web_id=7293202018252113450).

**Example**:

> “Going to a hostel alone doesn’t scare me. In da clerb we all fam.”

‍

## L

If you watch sports, you’ll be familiar with the concept of a “wins” (W) and “losses” (L) column. To say something is an L is **an abbreviation for “loss” or “losing,” or that something was an embarrassment.** ‍

**Example:**

> ‍ _“I tried to ask her out and she said no. The biggest L.”_ ‍

‍

## Let them cook

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792c75c07cd57c354557ab5_b92714ce-477e-46fd-a6ef-1b3f5979c42f.png)

The phrase “let them cook” **means stepping back to let someone continue what they’re doing**—either because it’s interesting or might lead to something great.

**Example:**

> “Damn. He just sacrificed his queen. He’s 100% going to lose this round of chess.”

> “He’s a chess prodigy, remember? Let him cook.”

‍

## Lore

If someone asks you about your “lore,” what they’re really asking for is **your backstory**. “Lore” could also be **general knowledge about a subject** such as [One Direction lore](https://www.tiktok.com/@bre.giglio/video/7429154668690820383) or [plant lore](https://www.tiktok.com/@justokayco/video/6952897180176764165).

**Example**:

> “My dad dropped the craziest lore yesterday. He told me he’d been married before my mom…for 10 years.”

‍

## Looksmaxxing

![Three male models](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792c7a0a7b6aa4d1733658d_654ab2f836d588dc55cca34b.jpeg)

“Looksmaxxing” is **the process of maximizing one’s physical attractiveness**. The trend is popular among teenage boys and idolizes conventional beauty standards: clear skin, defined muscles, sharp jawlines, and “hunter eyes” (almond-shaped eyes).

Looksmaxxers can enhance their appearance [in two ways](https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20240326-inside-looksmaxxing-the-extreme-cosmetic-social-media-trend):

• ”Softmaxxing:” gua shua, haircut, moisturizer, whitening strips, etc.

• ”Hardmaxxing:” cosmetic surgery, steroids, hair transplants, etc.

**Example**:

> “I used to be ugly. But then I tried this looksmaxxing thing for a few months and now I'm getting more replies to my DMs."

‍

## Lowkey

“Lowkey” can **describe something chill and understated** (e.g. “Don’t invite too many people to the party, it’s going to be lowkey”) or **to admit to something embarrassing** such as a [guilty pleasure](https://www.google.com/search?q=define+lowkey&rlz=1C5CHFA_enUS926US926&oq=define+lowkey&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyDggAEEUYORhGGPkBGIAEMgcIARAAGIAEMgkIAhAAGAoYgAQyCQgDEAAYChiABDIJCAQQABgKGIAEMgkIBRAAGAoYgAQyCggGEAAYChgWGB4yDQgHEAAYhgMYgAQYigUyDQgIEAAYhgMYgAQYigUyDQgJEAAYhgMYgAQYigXSAQgyMzE3ajBqNKgCALACAQ&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8#fpstate=ive&vld=cid:a6d7d5b7,vid:9C5nvWlKTOo,st:5)  (e.g. “I lowkey love the song 'One Less Lonely Girl.'”)

**Example**:

> “Lowkey I failed math twice in 8th grade. I had to do summer school to get into high school.”

‍

## Lock In

To “lock in” means to **focus and commit fully**. It's a way of saying you're "getting in the zone,” whether it be for a one-off activity or for a long-term commitment.

**Example**:

> “I’m locking in this 2025. Unlike last year, I’m going to go to the gym, reduce my screen time, and read more.”

‍

## Main Character Energy

You know that movie scene where the person is walking down the street in slow motion and everyone is staring at them? That’s main character energy — **when someone puts themselves first and the world revolves around them**. Far from conceited, this is a powerful compliment people give one another on TikTok.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“Ever since she got over her breakup, she’s been giving main character energy.”_

‍

## Math ain’t mathing

Your date cancels because of a family emergency…but their Instagram story literally shows them at Space Miami. A client claims they never opened your email…but your Mailtrack says otherwise.

These are classic examples of when the “math ain’t mathing”— **situations where things don’t add up or align with the facts**.

**Example**:

> “She says she’s broke but I saw her the other day with a $3,000 Prada bag. The math ain’t mathing.”

‍

## Mid

Mid is short for “mid-tier” or “mediocre” and is used for **when something is subpar**. It can be used as an adjective or a noun and cana be used to describe someone’s looks, a meal, or anything in between. But according to Urban Dictionary, it’s somewhat derogatory — the word is “used to insult or degrade an opposing opinion, labeling it as average or poor quality.”

**Example:**

> ‍ _“Yeah, I saw him on Hinge but he looked kind of mid to be honest.”_ ‍

‍

## Morning Shed

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792c911e743d8086c128f1b_75323593-6988-43af-b63a-478169996af9.png)

The “morning shed” is **a TikTok trend where people film videos of themselves removing layers of beauty and skincare products they slept in the night before**. The idea is the more products you use overnight, the more fresh-faced you’ll be in the morning.

**Example**:

> “Sorry I’m late. I had to do my morning shed and remove my jaw strap, silk bonnet, pimple patches, and under eye masks.”

‍

## OPP List

An “opp list” is **a list of sworn enemies or rivals** (“opp” is an abbreviation of “opponent”).

**Example**:

> “My kid told me I was at the top of her OPP list after I told them to do the dishes.”

‍

## Period

“Period” is **a strong emphasis to drive your point home** or **signals the end of the conversation**. It’s the equivalent of “There is nothing left to be said” or “I have nothing to add.”

**Example**:

> “'I Will Always Love You' by Whitney Houston is the best song of our generation. Period.”

‍

## Point of View (POV)

No need for you to be confused here — point of view means the same thing on TikTok as it does in real life. 😅 POV is used to **signal when the viewer should be watching the video from a specific perspective.**

However on TikTok, people often use “POV” for the “nostalgiacore” trend. This is when users try to **evoke a specific memory or common occurrence**, such as the POV of remembering what it was like to wake up early for school only for it to be a snow day (90’s babies will understand).

**Example:**

> ‍ _“_ [_#pov_](https://www.tiktok.com/@elongatedmusk/video/7157075564954701102?is_copy_url=1&is_from_webapp=v1&q=pov&t=1671126409478) _we have to come up with an alibi for our crime.”_ ‍

‍

## Pookie

In [the 1300s](https://catchwordbranding.com/catchthis/the-language-of-love-english-terms-of-endearment-through-the-ages/#:~:text=OG%20ENDEARMENTS,for%20more%20than%201%2C200%20years.), we had “poppet” and “honey.” In the 1800s, we had “honeybunch” and “buttercup.” And in the 2020s? We have “pookie.” The **term of endearment** skyrocketed this past year thanks to social media couple [Campbell and Jeff Pucket](https://mashable.com/article/pookie-jett-tiktok-wife-guy).

**Example**:

> “We’re going out to dinner tonight and pookie looks absolutely fire.”

‍

## Pick Me Girl

A “pick me girl” is **someone who claims they're “not like most girls” in an attempt to get attention and validation from men**. They might reject lipstick and heels, and would _never_ order a salad on a date (but rather a burger) since they’re “one of the guys.”

**Example:**

> ‍ _“She asked me how I could wear heels at the prom and not Converse like her, and I told her she was such a ‘pick me girl.’”_ ‍

‍

## Preen

Preen has two meanings:

1. To “ [preen](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/us/dictionary/english/preen#:~:text=If%20someone%20preens%20themselves%2C%20they,%5Bdisapproval%5D)” means **to obsessively perfect and polish your appearance**—to a point where it’s laughably over the top. It comes from the behavior of birds who meticulously clean their feathers with their beaks.

2. A “preen” refers to **a child under 13 who acts or dresses like a teenager** per [Urban Dictionary](https://www.urbandictionary.com/define.php?term=Preen).

**Example**:

> “My little sister asked to borrow my crop top and lipstick. She’s 9. She’s such a preen.”

‍

## Make it Make Sense

On TikTok, “make it make sense” is a phrase people use when **they’re confused and don’t understand how something happened**.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“Rachel got a 95 on her test and she didn’t even study. Make it make sense.”_ ‍

‍

## NPC

If you play video games, chances are you might already be familiar with this term. NPC stands for “Non-Playable Character” and are characters you interact with but aren’t controlled by a real person. These characters are just following a per-determined script and they do not have any agency of their own.

On TikTok, **NPC is a harsh slang word for someone who is “incapable of thinking for themselves” and regurgitates information**. There’s also a TikTok trend where people pretend to be NPCs, where they have deadpan expressions, glassy eyes, and repeat the same empty phrases.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“Bro, don’t be such an NPC and actually think about what you’re saying. You’re literally just regurgitating the echo chamber of your Twitter feed.”_ ‍

‍

## Ratio

A ratio has nothing to do with mathematics and instead everything to do with the comment section. On TikTok, saying “ratio” means **the original post has more replies than it does likes** OR that a reply has mor likes than the original post— a signal that **the original post is a bad take**.

Consider saying “ratio” as an alternative to the “dislike” button.

[**Example**](https://www.tiktok.com/@slushypriv/video/7062406855464668462?embed_source=70846776%2C120811592%2C120810756%3Bnull%3Bembed_masking&is_copy_url=1&is_from_webapp=v1&refer=embed&referer_url=wegotthiscovered.com%2Ftv%2Fwhat-does-ratio-mean-on-tiktok%2F&referer_video_id=6984795848299334918) **:**

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa5e9381088e9eab101_7pF4_9ZjWPGc35D_TOea_hj8DMylFQO_KikI7LvVHJxb-LCUGgQ0jE5fvAiDfSzaJhFXgy_F0nXEhvmM0laHrjqAmy_ZyQebTmoAvcPM6YEuRLeuDWdnt7VYbK7iMLckuu5IwLhI1QFdfvM9H7qbwl2dW0CalZJZNLy8FCSRlwIQBM46yedRbSICqt_SPg.png)

## Rent Free

When **someone cannnot get something out of their head, it lives there “rent free.”** This means it occupies your headspace because you’re too preoccupied with it.

This phrase can also be argumentative. Say a TikToker posts a video complaining about someone. A comment could say, “Damn, that person lives in your head rent free” — meaning their obsession with them is showing.

Example:

> ‍ _“My ex called me 46 times last night. I really live in his head rent free.”_ ‍

‍

## Rizz

Coined by [YouTuber Kai Cenat](https://www.tiktok.com/@vineetx_/video/7115468885683391750?is_from_webapp=v1&item_id=7115468885683391750&lang=en), **“rizz” is a male’s ability to impress a woman — also known as “game.”**

**Example:**

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa5ec64fb369a8ab12f_ijsX0i_RL2Y9H4Epa52xcUYZ-8GroPNgziU34N6yF76_ZvR_RuV5JhEYT2LVxzkHIqK-IjP64R5z9m0QY3v1dDNFjRdaQA1TI-v1GtAACgxq3rGJljFdDwO-PdL_PhKNx5qsqy2NI3UU0Lkuz5N-ZMt7CDy44LctUeZzEDXGr712DLIaErCpzZ3lfgPJlA.png)

## Romantasy

Are you a huge Harry Potter and Game of Thrones fan? Ever wished those stories had more romance and spice? Then [romantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_fantasy)— **a fiction sub-genre that blends fantasy and romance**—is probably your favorite thing right now.

**Example**:

> “‘Twilight' is the original romantasy. You just can’t top vampire Edward Cullen and werewolf Jacob Black fighting over Bella.”

‍

## Sigma

A “ [sigma](https://www.tiktok.com/@mr_lindsay_sped/video/7360461000694451487?lang=en)” is **an independent and self-reliant lone wolf who rejects traditional social hierarchies**. Think of them as a “cool” outsider—basically, what “all 10-year-olds think they are” as [Urban Dictionary](https://www.urbandictionary.com/define.php?term=Sigma) puts it.

**Example**:

> “Do these Pit Vipers make me look sigma?”

‍

## Simp

The popular definition of a “simp” **is someone (typically a male) who is desperate for the attention and validation of a woman** — to the point where they’ll become submissive. It usually has negative connotations and you can use it as both a verb and a noun.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“Is it bad that I simp for her?”_ ‍

‍

## Skibidi Toilet

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792caf675473fefdef7401c_6fcd6c7a-d9c8-49f3-ba1b-1e0abb42a2f5.png)

[Skibidi Toilet](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WePNs-G7puA) is a viral YouTube Shorts series by Georgian animator Alexey Gerasimov that chronicles a bizarre world where mobile toilets with human heads fight against mechanical humanoids.

If that sounds insane, that’s because it is. But that didn’t stop Skibidi Toilet and its 74 episodes from going mega-viral on TikTok. Now, skibidi—originally a useless filler word—has evolved into **Gen Alpha’s way of saying “cool.”**

**Example**:

> “Why are you wearing a button-up to school? You’re not skibidi.” **‍**

## **‍** Slop

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/6792cb472e93c5aef1618bac_38a6f9c2-5a44-45e1-ae41-2e669508adc3.png)

“Slop” isn't about unappetizing food. The term [describes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop#:~:text=It%20has%20been%20variously%20defined,increasingly%2C%20in%20search%20results%22.) **low-quality, unwanted AI-generated material increasingly found in our personal algorithm and search results**.

**Example**:

“Facebook is full of slop. All I found was images of Shrimp Jesus and users commenting ‘Amen.’”

‍

## Spicy

Nope, “spicy” isn’t slang for your taste buds. People on TikTok say “spicy” as slang for something **that is either sexual, mildly aggressive** (for example, [a hissing stray kitten](https://www.tiktok.com/@weatherman_catman/video/7091815133403499819?is_copy_url=1&is_from_webapp=v1&q=spicy%20meows&t=1671554052752)), **or controversial**. In this case, context is essential for this slang word.

‍

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa563703a609a742aa5_jWFaddGVxaFsg52fHaNkpa8HfVF3LjkTUpL9YKCxyMM6JvwGrgqphYNBfGdUD4e1nzkjn9ML5pgHeO7lkkMYX86_AqG_GZakeQIb6mrrXEtFHx_VbTSUSfqWenKO9_Wofl_NdGd5yFzp-14a1h9zaceg261jQVvszGIxv85BsTysb9ruiQJX0FQz6bhFLg.png)

**Example:**

> ‍ _“ACOTAR gets spicy!”_ ‍

‍

## Suspect

The “ [Suspect Challenge](https://www.today.com/life/suspect-challenge-tiktok-rcna178814)” is a TikTok trend where **one person jogs and the other person filming playfully roasts them** in the form of a police broadcast.

**Example**:

> “ [Suspect](https://www.tiktok.com/@kyleandjade_/video/7439823959794912558) is balding in his 30s and tries to cover it up with a durag.”

‍

## Tea

This slang isn’t exactly new, but it’s more prevalent than ever. “Tea” is slang for gossip, and if someone says it’ll be “served piping hot” that means it’s _particularly_ juicy. But you can also say “tea” with the following emojis: 🫖and ☕.

**Example:**

> “ _You were at the party last Saturday right? Omg, spill the tea please.”_ ‍

‍

## Unalive

“Unalive” is **a substitute for kill**. Oftedn used ironically, it’s a way to circumvent TikTok which will flag or remove content that explicitly mentions death-related incidences.

**Example:**

> ‍ _“I was supposed to be back three hours ago, my mom is absolutely going to unalive me.”_ ‍

‍

## Vibe Check

A “vibe check” is the Gen-Z version of asking “What’s going on?” or “How is everyone?” If someone “passes” the vibe check it’s a good thing — it means that person has a “vibe” and is pleasant to be around.

**Example:**

‍

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa5f946cc9ea1cd040d_MkAvcx2BD0aa94qyFyDAFjIT0G7q-nec3RkcSB1cy_dA0tpqKzl-jD9mcc7tivxvj0e-JdZ7BH9U2eYoOu3lx01hlG_tjduca004RoZv7mC12GRZ6qCD_oBcXeokc4wcb_S_a5JnueGXyFFFNsNH3ey1CeNrWZCgGTSbMHNWEzf3fiwsxn1AZCvcqpI7Rg.png)

## W

In short, **“w” is an abbreviation for  “win.”** It's a way of saying that something was a good achievement, something someone should be proud of. You can use it to describe just about anything, from music, to outfits, to food, or someone’s lifestyle.

**Example:**

‍

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/60fae5367236bf2f33648a4f/63a32fa5dcb75c813b0c77a0_rAHhOjc8KQjIhKWB2whOjp44t3lmLE-6yDB0yiLeLxmBxr7KzxZZYPAERpsyK62v1ywSpFTKAPSzMWddX_Ew7iangnE0D_I9O1ImaTT2VIJgN7p4QmXAsaK3guL3qboDqKZ6rmX0UREUgHwvV0wgdy7JL40FZ8vXrd9KjAi7dClbXcTw6-6dqDVSuwuqng.png)

## Yap

To “yap” **means to chatter on–usually about something of little importance**. If someone calls you a “yapper,” what they really mean is that you love to talk (maybe a little too much.) However, it can also have a positive connotation sometimes, describing the pleasant activity of talking a lot with a friend.

**Example**:

> “I’m the [biggest yapper](https://www.tiktok.com/@diaryofad2dsaleswoman/video/7376703649793264939?q=yapper&t=1735829765604) on the planet. That’s why I love working in sales and sales loves me.”

‍

## Zesty

“ [Zesty](https://www.wikihow.com/What-Does-Zesty-Mean-Tiktok)” is a derogatory term used to describe a man who dresses and acts in a stereotypically feminine way. Once a positive word for someone energetic, in the past year it has shifted to a negative—and is often used to bully someone.

**Example**:

> “Why did you paint your nails? Bro is mad zesty.”

[Skip to content](https://bamfuzzle.com/blog/2026-internet-slang-terms-explained/#main)

No results

[![Bamfuzzle](https://bamfuzzle.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Bamfuzzle-Logo.png)![Bamfuzzle](https://bamfuzzle.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Bamfuzzle-Logo.png)](https://bamfuzzle.com/)

![Crashing Out edited](https://bamfuzzle.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Crashing-Out_-edited.jpg)

## What Counts as “Internet Slang” in 2026, and How This List Was Chosen

Internet slang, for the purposes of this list, means words or phrases that spread primarily through short-form video and comment sections rather than television, movies, or traditional media, within the current cycle. To make the cut, a term had to be widely used across TikTok, X, and Instagram in 2026, have a traceable origin, and exist for a reason other than mocking someone’s appearance or behavior.

That last criterion knocked a few terms off the list that show up on other slang guides. Words that exist mainly to shame someone’s body or dating history got cut, even though they’re common, because “common” and “worth repeating” aren’t the same thing. A term earns a spot here by describing a mood, a behavior, or a shared experience, not by giving people a sharper way to insult a stranger.

Here’s the full cheat sheet before the deep dives, so you can scan it or hand it to an AI assistant and get the whole picture in one pass.

| Term | One-Line Meaning | Origin Type | Still Rising or Fading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6-7 | Deliberately meaningless number used as a comedic interruption | Song / sports moment | Fading, but still everywhere |
| Delulu | Being delusional about a crush, job, or fantasy outcome | K-pop stan culture | Still rising |
| Crashing Out | Having a visible emotional or behavioral meltdown | Meme / general slang shift | Still rising |
| Aura Farming | Acting deliberately cool, often self-aware and mocked | Sports / gaming clips | Rising |
| Canon Event | An unavoidable, defining life moment | Fandom / superhero discourse | Steady |
| Chopped | Looking bad or having no real chance | General slang | Steady |
| Mewing | Tongue-posture technique claimed to sharpen the jawline | Orthodontic method, memed | Fading |
| Unc | Someone acting older or more out of touch than their age | Black American English | Steady |
| Brat | Confidently unbothered and unapologetically messy | Pop culture moment | Fading from peak, still used |
| Biblically Accurate | Something strange, overwhelming, or unsettling | Religious art meme | Steady |
| Beige Flag | A quirk that’s neither a red flag nor a green flag | Dating content escalation | Rising |
| NPC Energy | Acting scripted or blending into the background | Livestream trend, gaming | Steady |
| Brain Rot | Low-value content, or the foggy feeling from consuming too much | Self-aware scrolling joke | Still rising |
| Skibidi | Absurdist filler word with no fixed meaning | Animated meme series | Rising |

![Internet Slang](https://bamfuzzle.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Internet-Slang-1024x576.jpg)

## “6-7” (Also Written 67): What the Number Actually Means

“6-7” is a deliberately meaningless number that gets shouted whenever someone says a number close to six or seven, or mentions height, age, or a test score. The joke only works because it doesn’t mean anything specific.

The term’s spread is tied to a song and artist that put the phrase in rotation, plus a basketball player whose height became attached to the joke, which is part of why the number stuck instead of fading immediately. The entire appeal is that it’s vague enough to interrupt almost any conversation.

You’d hear it like this: someone says “I’m turning 27 next week” and a kid across the room yells “6-7!” for no real reason at all.

“6-7” has a cousin term, “41,” which functions more like a contradiction or an alternate answer than its own separate joke. Think of it as the “actually” version rather than a standalone punchline.

![6 7](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20535'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## What Does “Delulu” Mean, and Why Did a Dictionary Name It Word of the Year?

“Delulu” is short for delusional, and it almost always describes someone’s own overly optimistic or unrealistic belief, usually about a crush, a job offer, or a fantasy outcome that isn’t grounded in reality. It grew out of K-pop stan culture on Twitter before crossing into everyday use, and a major dictionary later recognized it as a word of the year, which should be verified against the dictionary’s own announcement before you cite the date anywhere official.

What makes “delulu” different from a plain insult is the tone. People use it about themselves constantly, almost as a badge of honor, the way someone might say “I know this is delusional, but I think he’s texting back.”

A typical use looks like this: “I’m delulu but I think my landlord is going to lower my rent this year.”

![Delulu](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20575'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## “Crashing Out”: The 2026 Term for Losing Your Composure in Public

To “crash out,” or to have a “crash out,” means having a visible emotional or behavioral meltdown, usually set off by stress, jealousy, or a breakup playing out somewhere public. It’s more intense and more public than older phrases like “big mad,” which tended to describe quiet, simmering anger rather than an actual visible spiral.

You’d use it like this: “She saw his location was at his ex’s apartment and immediately crashed out in the group chat.” The term works because it names a very specific escalation point, the moment private frustration turns into a public performance, and that specificity is exactly why it replaced vaguer older phrases.

![Crashing Out edited](https://bamfuzzle.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Crashing-Out_-edited.jpg)

## What Is “Aura Farming”? The Slang Behind Every Slow-Motion Sports Clip

“Aura farming” describes deliberately acting or moving in a way designed to look effortlessly cool, and it’s mocked about as often as it’s admired. The phrase comes out of sports and gaming clip culture, where “aura” started as a genuine compliment about someone’s presence before “farming” got added on to call out people who were clearly trying too hard for the clip.

A typical use: “That celebration was pure aura farming, he practiced that walk in the mirror.” The double meaning is the point. The same clip can be praised for having genuine aura and roasted for farming it, sometimes in the same comment section.

![Aura Farming](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## “Canon Event”: Why Fans Use a Comic Book Term for Real Life

A “canon event” is a moment framed as an unavoidable, defining part of someone’s story, borrowed from fandom language about what officially “counts” as real within a fictional universe. It moved out of superhero and franchise discourse and into everyday use once people started applying it to their own lives.

You’d hear it as: “Getting my heart broken in college was a canon event, I wouldn’t be who I am without it.”

![Canon Event edited](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20900'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## “Chopped”: The Blunt Way 2026 Describes Someone’s Odds

Calling someone or something “chopped” means it looks bad or has no real shot, most often used about a person’s looks or how a situation is likely to turn out. The word carries a real edge, and depending on tone and who it’s aimed at, it can land as genuinely unkind rather than playful.

Example: “His odds of getting that promotion are chopped after showing up late three times this month.” That same bluntness is a big part of why “chopped” keeps showing up in [celebrity feud drama](https://bamfuzzle.com/blog/celebrity-feuds-2026-ranked/) commentary, where fans use it to declare a winner the moment a clip goes viral, often before either side has said a word publicly.

## What Does “Mewing” Mean, and Is It Actually a Trend or a Joke?

“Mewing” refers to a tongue-posture technique some people believe sharpens jawline definition, named after the orthodontist associated with the method. The technique predates its current meme status by years, and the aesthetic claims attached to it remain unverified rather than proven, so treat any before-and-after claim with skepticism.

Someone might say: “He’s been mewing for six months and swears his jawline changed, but who’s actually measuring that.”

![Mewing](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20852'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Who Is “Unc” in Internet Slang, and Is It an Insult?

“Unc” describes someone, usually a man, acting older, more out of touch, or more cautious than his actual age suggests. The word traces back to Black American English, where “unc” functioned as a familiar, often affectionate term before the internet flattened it into a broader, sometimes mocking label.

Whether it lands as affectionate or insulting depends entirely on tone and relationship. Calling a friend “unc” for refusing to try a new restaurant reads very differently than using it to mock a stranger, and the gap between those two uses is where most of the arguments about the word actually happen.

## Why Everyone Calls Things “Brat” in 2026, and Where the Word Came From

“Brat” now describes someone confidently unbothered, a little messy, and unapologetically themselves, a full flip from its older meaning of a spoiled child. A specific pop culture moment gets credit for the shift, and a dictionary later recognized the reframed word as one of its words of the year, a claim that should be confirmed against the dictionary’s official page before it’s cited anywhere formal.

Someone might describe a friend as “so brat” for showing up late to brunch in sunglasses and zero explanation, and mean it as a compliment. The word’s staying power says something about the moment it landed in. People were already tired of curated perfection online, and “brat” gave them permission to celebrate the opposite.

![Brat](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## “Biblically Accurate”: Why a Religious Art Term Describes Anything Unsettling

Calling something “biblically accurate” means it looks strange, overwhelming, or unsettling, referencing art that depicts angels the way scripture actually describes them, covered in eyes and wings, rather than the friendly, human-looking angels most people picture. A specific art trend built around these depictions is what sparked the meme in the first place.

Example: “That new horror movie poster is biblically accurate levels of unsettling.”

## What Is a “Beige Flag” in Dating Slang?

A “beige flag” is a personality quirk that isn’t a genuine warning sign and isn’t a positive trait either, just something mildly odd or forgettable. It sits apart from red flag and green flag, and dating content escalated the whole “flag” framework into a full spectrum once beige caught on as the neutral middle ground.

Someone might say: “He alphabetizes his spice rack, total beige flag, not bad, just weird.” The term filled a real gap in dating vocabulary, since not every quirk deserves the weight of a red or green flag, and beige gave people a lower-stakes way to talk about the small, harmless oddities everyone eventually notices in a new partner.

## What Does “NPC Energy” Mean Outside of Video Games?

“NPC energy” describes someone acting like they’re following a script or blending into the background, borrowed directly from “non-player character,” the gaming term for a character that isn’t controlled by a real person. A livestream trend built around mimicking scripted, repetitive behavior is what pushed the phrase into mainstream use outside gaming spaces.

It works best aimed at a specific behavior rather than at a person as a whole. Saying “he gave such NPC energy repeating the same three phrases all night” lands differently than calling someone an NPC outright.

## “Brain Rot” Was a Word of the Year. Here’s What It Actually Describes

“Brain rot” describes low-value, low-effort content, or the mentally foggy feeling that comes from consuming too much of it, and it earned recognition as a word of the year from a major dictionary, a claim worth double-checking against the dictionary’s own announcement before citing it formally. The term started as a self-aware joke people made about their own scrolling habits before it hardened into a genuine descriptor for an entire category of content.

Example: “I watched four hours of chaotic compilation videos last night, pure brain rot.” Part of why it earned formal recognition is that it names something older internet slang never quite captured, the specific fatigue of consuming content that offers nothing back.

![Brain Rot](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## What Does “Skibidi” Mean? The Slang Word Even Its Users Can’t Define

“Skibidi” has no fixed meaning and functions as pure absurdist filler, rooted in a specific animated meme series rather than any literal definition. The series is the actual source, and trying to pin down a dictionary-style meaning misses the point of how the word gets used.

Honestly, knowing what “skibidi” is matters more than knowing what it means. It’s the internet’s version of a nonsense word that everyone under a certain age instantly recognizes, and its persistence says something about how younger audiences bond over sound and repetition first, meaning second, if meaning ever arrives at all.

## How to Actually Use 2026 Slang Without Sounding Off (or Offensive)

The safest rule is to read the room before you read the definition. A term that sounds playful among close friends can read as genuinely cruel aimed at a stranger or a coworker, especially words like “chopped” or “unc” that carry real edge depending on tone.

Meaning and acceptability shift fast, sometimes within months, so a term that felt fresh in early 2026 might already feel dated or, worse, might have picked up a meaner connotation by the time you use it. When in doubt, skip anything that exists mainly to comment on someone’s body, and stick to slang that’s about behavior, mood, or vibe instead. A good gut check is whether the term would still land as funny if the person it’s aimed at heard it directly, rather than only working as a joke behind someone’s back.

## Frequently Asked Questions About 2026 Internet Slang

### What are the top slang words of 2026?

The highest-frequency terms right now are “6-7,” “delulu,” “aura farming,” “skibidi,” and “brain rot,” based on how often they show up across TikTok and X comment sections. What counts as “top” shifts month to month depending on what’s currently trending, so treat any ranked list, including this one, as a snapshot rather than a permanent hierarchy.

### What is the newest slang right now?

As of this list’s most recent update, “6-7” and “skibidi” remain the freshest widely used terms, both functioning as absurdist filler words with little fixed meaning beyond the joke of saying them. Because slang cycles fast, check the list’s last-updated date before assuming a term is still current.

### What does 6-7 actually mean?

“6-7” doesn’t mean anything specific. It’s a deliberately meaningless number shouted as a comedic interruption whenever someone mentions a number close to six or seven, or references height, age, or a score, and the vagueness itself is the entire joke.

### Is “unc” an insult?

It depends entirely on tone and relationship. Between friends, “unc” usually lands as affectionate teasing about acting older or more cautious than your actual age. Aimed at a stranger with a harsher tone, it can read as genuinely dismissive, so context matters more than the word itself.

### What slang should you avoid using?

Avoid terms that exist mainly to comment on someone’s body, appearance, or promiscuity, even if they’re common across other slang lists. These words are common because they’re used to mock people, not because they add anything useful to a sentence, and skipping them costs you nothing conversationally.

## Closing Thoughts

Slang cycles fast enough that any list claiming to be complete is lying to you a little. What holds up is the pattern underneath the individual words: a lot of 2026 slang started as an inside joke in a specific fandom, sport, or dating context before the algorithm dragged it into everyone’s comment section.

This list gets a quarterly refresh as terms fade and new ones take their place, so bookmark it rather than screenshotting it. Fandom culture keeps feeding this list more than people realize, which is part of why [K-pop comeback chaos](https://bamfuzzle.com/blog/kpop-comebacks-2026-ranked-by-chaos/) is worth reading next if you want to see where a lot of this year’s slang actually got its start, sound and moment first, dictionary definition a distant second.
